en: H 63a6; C 328c5 (0) What is the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitā bhūmi*)?
The summary verse (*uddāna*) states:
the enumeration, its establishment, mental attention (*manaskāra*), and the signs (*nimitta*).
And the compendium of the sūtras shall be the final, diverse [section].

The stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitā bhūmiḥ*) is to be understood, in brief, by way of its enumeration, its formal establishment, the distinctions of mental attention (*manasikāra*), the distinctions of signs (*nimitta*), and the compendium of the sūtras. What is the enumeration?
In brief, the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitā bhūmi*) is fourfold, namely: dhyāna, liberation (*vimokṣa*), meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and attainment (*samāpatti*).
What is dhyāna?
There are four dhyānas:

[The first dhyāna] is born of seclusion, with applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*); [the second] is born of concentration (*samādhija*), without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarkam avicāram*); [the third is] free from joy (*niṣprītika*); and [the fourth is] purified by equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣāsmṛtipariśuddha*). (H 63a7; C 328c15) What is liberation (*vimokṣa*)?
There are eight liberations:
"One possessing form sees forms" is the first liberation.
"Being internally percipient of the formless, one sees forms externally" is the second liberation.
"Having realized the beautiful liberation with the body and having attained it, one dwells therein" is the third liberation.

The sphere of infinite space … the sphere of infinite consciousness … the sphere of nothingness … the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception … having personally realized the cessation of perception and feeling with the body and having attained it, he dwells therein: this is the eighth liberation. What is concentration?
Emptiness, the wishless, and the signless. Furthermore, there are three concentrations:
with applied thought and sustained thought, without applied thought and with sustained thought only, and without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Again there are three: the limited, the exalted, and the immeasurable. Again there are three:
Accompanied by joy, accompanied by pleasure, and accompanied by equanimity. Furthermore, there is concentration cultivated in one part, and concentration cultivated in both parts.
Again, there is concentration accompanied by the cultivation of the four concentrations.
Furthermore, there is the noble concentration consisting of five knowledges;
furthermore, there is the noble concentration consisting of five factors;
furthermore, there is the noble concentration itself together with its proximate cause and its requisites.
Furthermore, there is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Furthermore, there is the concentration of one in training (*śaikṣa*), the concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the concentration of neither one in training nor one beyond training.
What is meditative attainment (*samāpatti*)?

The five attainments of vision (*darśana-samāpatti*), the eight attainments of the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana-samāpatti*), the ten attainments of the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana-samāpatti*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñā-samāpatti*).
(2.0.0) What is their formal establishment?

(2.0.1) Why, moreover, is only this considered the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitā bhūmi*), and not even that one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) which exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
Because this concentration is brought forth by non-regret, joy, rapture, tranquility, and bliss, and is not of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Yet, it is not that there is no correct contemplation of the Dharma within the desire realm.
In that regard, the first dhyāna is called "the joy of seclusion" (*pravivekaprīti*).

For one who dwells having realized that [state], five factors are abandoned, namely: mental pleasure associated with sensual desire, mental pain associated with sensual desire, mental pleasure associated with the unwholesome, mental pain associated with the unwholesome, and equanimity associated with the unwholesome.
Five factors reach the fulfillment of cultivation:
Joy, rapture, pliancy, bliss, and meditative concentration. (H 63b5;
C 329a10) What is mental well-being associated with sensual desires?

It is that mental well-being which arises in dependence upon the five strands of sensual desire—whether they are being acquired, have already been acquired, or are currently being enjoyed—and which occurs when one recollects those very same objects as seen, heard, or experienced.

(2.1.1.2) What is mental distress associated with sensual desires? It is that mental distress which arises in dependence upon not obtaining those very five strands of sensual pleasure, or failing to obtain their enjoyment again after having obtained them, or through the loss, departure, or destruction of what has been obtained. (2.1.1.3) What is joy associated with the unwholesome?
For example, here a certain person commits killing, up to and including holding wrong views, together with pleasure and together with mental gladness.

(H 63b7; C 329a16, 2.1.1.4) What is dejection associated with the unwholesome? For example, here a certain person commits killing, up to and including holding wrong views, together with pain and together with dejection.
(2.1.1.5) What is equanimity associated with the unwholesome?

It is when, for example, a certain person—whether he be a king, a royal official, or whoever holds authority over someone else, such as a teacher or one in the position of a teacher—himself has no desire to commit the evil act of taking life, yet he looks on with indifference while it is being committed by his subordinates; he does not prevent it, nor does he establish them in discipline. Through that indifference, the performance of that action occurs, and he [partakes in] that...
One experiences karma, which does not remain hidden;

and there is that equanimity associated with the acceptance of its non-abandonment while one is reflecting upon and examining what is wholesome; and there is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling for one who is engaged in unwholesome conduct.

(2.1.2.1) What is *prāmodya* (joy)? It is the state of mental gladness, joy, and fitness of mind that arises from observing the thoroughly purified stage of equipment (*saṃbhārabhūmi*) of one who is pure from the beginning, preceded by freedom from regret. (2.1.2.2) What is *prīti* (rapture)?
That which is joy, gladness, mental well-being, and fitness of mind, preceded by correct application.
(H 64a2; C 329a27, 2.1.2.3) What is pliancy (*prasrabdhi*)? It is the serviceability of body and mind resulting from the departure of rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*).
H 64a3; C 329a28 (2.1.2.4) What is happiness (*sukha*)?
It is that physical and mental bliss which is free from affliction and is the bliss of liberation for one whose mind is thus pliable (*karmanya*).
For that heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to that side has been removed, and there is liberation from those secondary defilements (*upakleśa*).
H 64a3; C 329b1 (2.1.2.5) What is concentration (*samādhi*)?
It is the one-pointedness of mind (*cetas aikāgrya*) of one who correctly contemplates the object of focus.

H 64a3; C 329b2 (2.1.2.6.1) Regarding the untainted application (*anāsrava-prayoga*), the Blessed One first spoke of concentration and afterwards of liberation; for by the power of concentration once it has been accomplished, there is simply the liberation of the mind from the afflictions (*kleśa*).

(2.1.2.6.2) However, regarding practice that is still associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), he first mentions liberation and afterwards concentration, because the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśaprahāṇa*) is the fruit of the mental application of the culmination of practice (*prayoganiṣṭhāmanasikāra*), and [this refers to] the attainment of fundamental concentration (*maulasamādhi*).

(2.1.2.6.3) He speaks of both concentration and liberation simultaneously; for example, that concentration which is accompanied by liberation within that very same mental application of the culmination of practice.
In this context, there are five hindrances that are obstructions to the attainment of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samāpatti*), which act as obstacles at the time of entering meditative absorption:

the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), and the hindrances of ill-will, lethargy-and-drowsiness, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt (*vyāpāda-styānamiddha-auddhatya-kaukṛtya-vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*).
What is sensual desire?

For one who pursues an attractive sign, it is the desire to see, up to the desire to touch, the five strands of sensual pleasure; or, for one who recollects what was previously experienced, it is the desire to conceptualize.

(H 64a6; C 329b14) What is ill-will (*vyāpāda*)? It is the resentment of the mind arising from receiving an admonition from fellow practitioners of the holy life, or from recollecting some cause of hostility such as a particular harm, or the desire of one wishing to inflict harm.
That very resentment of the mind which arises for one who repeatedly applies discursive thought (*vitarka*) and sustained reflection (*vicāra*) toward the object of aversion (*pratighanimitta*).

(2.2.1.3.1) What is lethargy (*styāna*)? It is the state of one engaged in abandonment (*prahāṇa*) who, having encountered any one of the following—failure in morality and so forth, lack of guarding the doors of the sense faculties, eating to excess, lack of application to wakefulness, or dwelling without clear comprehension—[becomes overcome by it].
What is torpor (*middha*)? It is the dullness and unwieldiness of body and mind that is conducive to the arising of all afflictions. What is torpor?
It is the contraction of the mind.
(2.2.1.3.3) *Styāna* (sloth) destroys the application for abandonment by giving rise to afflictions, whereas *middha* (torpor) does so by causing the contraction of the mind.
Therefore, both are said to constitute a single hindrance (*nivaraṇa*).
*Styāna* is due to a lack of functional pliability and a state of torpor, while *middha* is due to mental contraction and a state of torpor.
Furthermore, for other afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), there is no proximate condition for their arising as close as that of torpor (*middha*).
Other afflictions and secondary afflictions may or may not arise, but for one who has become drowsy, torpor necessarily arises. (H 64b1; C 329b28) What is restlessness (*auddhatya*)?

That lack of tranquility and mental agitation which arises from reflecting upon or being reminded of discursive thoughts concerning relatives, discursive thoughts concerning one’s native land, or discursive thoughts concerning the gods, or from recollecting or being reminded of former instances of laughing, playing, sporting, and enjoying oneself—that is [restlessness].
(H 64b2; C 329c1) What is remorse?
As he dwells on those very thoughts concerning relatives and so forth:

"Why have I been separated from those relatives; why have I not gone to that country; or why have I left that country and come here, where such kinds of solid food are eaten, such drinks are drunk, and where such requisites as robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick are obtained?"
"Why have I gone forth as a renunciant while still so young? I shall remain [in the world] until I reach old age! Or, recollecting former laughter, play, and the like:

"Why is it that at the time when I ought to dwell devoted to play, delight, adornment, and social gatherings, I must instead depart from my unwilling kinsmen, whose throats are choked with tears and whose faces are weeping?"
“Has he gone forth?”—the mental impression, distress, remorse, and regret that arise through such a cause as this.

And for this very reason, because they share the same basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*) and remorse (*kaukṛtya*) are treated as a single hindrance, the “hindrance of restlessness-and-remorse,” and thus spoken of.

Furthermore, regarding what ought to be done or what ought not to be done, whether one has performed it or not performed it as appropriate, [the thought arises]: “I have not done what should be done; I have done what should not be done. First of all...

Setting aside the remorse that has already arisen, there is another synonym for the hindrance of remorse (*kaukṛtyanivaraṇa*): when one is unable to dispel that very same obsession with remorse (*kaukṛtyaparyavasthāna*), there subsequently arises a continuous mental preoccupation, a brooding, a remorse, or a regret.
Furthermore, that remorse which is not based on a proper ground and that which is the latter type of remorse do not share the same objective basis as restlessness (*auddhatya*).

Moreover, just as that [restlessness] causes a lack of tranquility through its mode of agitation, so too does this [regret] do so through its mode of dejection; therefore, this too has been described by him in conjunction with that.
(H 64b5; C 329c19) What is doubt (*vicikitsā*)?
It is to have hesitation and doubt regarding the Teacher, or regarding the Dharma, the training, the instruction, or the realization.
For one who has thus fallen into doubt and uncertainty, that mind does not incline toward ardor, application, abandonment, or seclusion.

Whether he doubts and is uncertain regarding the past— just as with the past, so it is with the future and the present— or whether he doubts and is uncertain regarding the truths such as suffering, that state of duality in the mind, that hesitation, that indecision, is doubt.
(2.2.2.1.1) What is the nutriment for the hindrance of sensual desire?
There is the beautiful;
therein, there is improper mental attention and frequent cultivation thereof.
In that regard, what is the beautiful (*śubha*)?

It is that which is the foremost, excellent, and sublime among sensual pleasures (*kāma*); for one who is detached from this, detachment from other, even inferior things, follows as a matter of course—just as when a great wrestler is defeated, the defeat of his other opponents is already accomplished.
And what, then, is that?

That beauty associated with women, which is comprised of eight factors— by means of which eight factors a woman binds a man, namely: by dancing, singing, laughing, gazing, complexion, touch, attire, and the breaking of wounds—
is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire and for the increase of arisen sensual desire.
(2.2.2.1.2) What is non-nutriments? There is the meditation on the foul; therein, there is appropriate mental attention and frequent cultivation.
What, then, is that?
It is as follows: the livid corpse and so forth.
One contemplates this very body as full of various kinds of impurities.
In this way, one contemplates the internal body as impure.
Furthermore, one contemplates the external body as impure by means of its impurity, such as the livid state (*vinīlaka*) and so forth.
These two constitute the entirety of that which is impure.
This is the non-nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire and for the abandoning of arisen sensual desire.
Therein, through mental attention, there is non-arising; through frequent practice, there is abandoning.
In the dark side, however, through mental attention, there is arising; through frequent practice, there is further increase, growth, and expansion.
(2.2.2.2.1) What is the nutriment of ill-will? There is resentment, there is the cause of resentment; therein, improper mental attention is practiced frequently.
In that context, resentment (*pratigha*) is the mental hostility arising from an injury.
That very injury, when accompanied by improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), serves as the cause for resentment, as in the case of the nine bases of resentment.
(H 65a3; C 330a16) What is non-nutriment (*anāhāra*)?

There is loving-kindness (*maitrī*); therein lies the frequent practice of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśomanaskāra*). Furthermore, it is characterized by the bringing about of happiness for others and is encompassed by the power of cultivation (*bhāvanābala*).
The power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyānabala*) is also his non-nutriment, being comprised within the discipline that subdues the nine types of malice.
That by which the abandonment of the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpādanivaraṇa*) occurs is precisely what was taught in the Sūtra.
(H 65a4; C 330a21) What is the nutriment of the hindrance of sloth and torpor (*styānamiddhanivaraṇa*)?
There is darkness;
therein, improper mental attention is practiced frequently.
What is the lack of nutriment?
There is light;
therein lies the frequent practice of appropriate mental attention.
In that regard, light is threefold:
It consists of the light that is the antidote to darkness, the light of the Dharma, and the light of the physical basis.

Among these, the light that is the antidote to darkness pertains to the night, such as the moon, the stars, and so forth; it pertains to the day, such as the sun; and it pertains to both, such as the light of fire, jewels, and the like.

Therein, the light of the Dharma is when someone here reflects upon the teachings as they were received, contemplated, and realized, or cultivates the recollection of the Buddha and the other [jewels].
In that context, light based on a physical support (*āśrayāloka*) is, for example, that of beings who possess their own radiance.

In that regard, as an antidote to the first type of light, three kinds of darkness are to be understood: namely, the darkness of night, the darkness of clouds, and the darkness of concealment, such as that found in caves and similar places.

As an opposition to the light of the Dharma, there are three masses of darkness; for, not understanding those phenomena as they truly are, one doubts and wavers regarding the past, the future, and the present, as well as regarding the qualities of a Buddha and so forth.
In this regard, both that ignorance and that doubt are called the "mass of darkness."

Furthermore, as the counteragent to the analytical insight (*pratyavekṣā*) that has been attained, sloth and torpor (*styānamiddha*) are darkness, for by means of them there is no discernment of those phenomena (*taddharmāprasaṃkhyāna*).
(H 65a7; C 330b7) What is the nourishment (*āhāra*) of the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*auddhatyakaukṛtyanivaraṇa*)?
There are discursive thoughts regarding relatives and so forth, and one becomes a recollector of former laughter, play, and the like.
In that regard, it is the frequent practice of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
Therein, based on the prosperity or adversity, the union or separation of kinsmen, that which arises as a state of joy or dejection—a directing or non-directing of the mind—is what is meant.
Likewise, based on the prosperity and so forth of countries, the "thought concerning countries" (*janapadavitarka*) is to be understood in detail as previously described.
What is the reflection on immortality (*amaravitarka*)?
It is the application of the mind characterized by joy or dejection, based upon youth or old age, or that which is to be done for oneself or for others; such is the detailed explanation.
What is called "laughter" (*hasita*) is when someone, on account of a riddle or a shared conversation, laughs showing their teeth, chuckles, or exults with cries of joy.
In that context, "play" (*krīḍita*) refers to playing with dice, balls, jewels, or anything else of a similar kind.

"Amusement" (*ramita*) is the delight in enjoyment through mutual indulgence or the enjoyment of sense objects; it is also the delight in dwelling together, such as through living in the same place or conversing.

In that regard, "serving" refers to, for example, taking the hand, taking the arm, taking the braid of hair, or touching or stroking any various part of the body; or embracing, kissing, looking [lustfully], or whatever other similar acts of service there may be. (H 65b3; C 330b20) What is non-nutritive?
There is calm abiding (*śamatha*); therein, there is the frequent practice of appropriate mental attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*).
In this context, calm abiding refers to the ninefold stability of the mind and those factors conducive to calm abiding.

Furthermore, whatever things are provocative of spiritual urgency (*saṃvejana*), such as one’s own misfortune, the misfortune of others, one’s own prosperity, and the prosperity of others—by means of which the mind becomes stirred, terrified, and enters into a state of spiritual urgency, and thereby abides in tranquility.
(H 65b4; C 330b25) What is the nourishment for the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*)?
There are three time periods;
therein, there is the frequent practice of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
"Did I indeed exist in the past time? and so forth, as detailed previously.
This improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is comprised of inconceivable points.
Furthermore, the inconceivable points are as follows: reflection on the self (*ātmacintā*), reflection on sentient beings (*sattvacintā*), and reflection on the world (*lokacintā*).
Among these, reflection on the self with respect to the internal [basis] concerns the self across the [three] times.
Contemplation of sentient beings is based upon [the contemplation of] sentient beings; contemplation of the world is based upon the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world:
"The world is eternal," "it is non-eternal," "it is both eternal and non-eternal," "it is neither eternal nor non-eternal," and so forth.
What is non-nutriment? It is this conditionality, dependent origination; therein, there is thorough mental attention and frequent cultivation.

For one who perceives that there is only phenomena and only the cause of phenomena, as well as only suffering and only the cause of suffering, that ignorance which has its source in improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) does not arise with respect to the three times, and having arisen, it is abandoned. In this context, both improper mental attention and the non-attention to what is proper— taken together— are called "improper mental attention."

H 65b6; C 330c10 (2.2.2.6.2) Whatever is appropriate in a given case, that should be understood as being present therein; for example, in darkness, there is appropriate mental attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) through the application of the perception of light, but not inappropriate mental attention;
likewise, in other cases, there exists mental attention directed toward something else.
In this regard, the first dhyāna should be understood as having five factors:
applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
The second [dhyāna] has four factors:
Internal clarity, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind.
The third [dhyāna] has five factors: equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind.
The fourth [dhyāna] has four factors: purity of equanimity, purity of mindfulness, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and one-pointedness of mind.

(H 66a1; C 330c19) In that regard, in the first dhyāna, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) function for the purpose of grasping the object; concentration (*samādhi*), however, serves as their support; and joy (*prīti*) functions for the purpose of experiencing the object.
Bliss is for the purpose of removing coarseness (*dauṣṭhulya*).

In the second dhyāna, internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is for the purpose of grasping the object, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is for the purpose of providing a basis for internal clarity;
the remainder is as before.
In the third dhyāna, equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension function for the purpose of grasping the object, while concentration functions as its support;
the remainder is as before.
In the fourth dhyāna, the purity of equanimity and the purity of mindfulness function for the purpose of grasping the object, while concentration functions as their support.
The remainder is as before.
(2.3.3) Even though other factors are present, these alone constitute the constituent parts (*aṅga*) because they are primary and because they are beneficial to those who practice meditation.
(2.3.4) For what reason is the first dhyāna accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*)?
For in this way, one reviles the desire realm and enters the first dhyāna, yet does not perceive any fault in those applied and sustained thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*);
or rather, in the second dhyāna, one perceives a fault in them, and thus, through their subsiding, there is the second dhyāna.

Just as in the second dhyāna there is the subsiding of applied and sustained thought due to seeing their faults, so too in the third dhyāna there is the subsiding of joy (*prīti*) due to seeing its faults.
Then follows the attainment of the third dhyāna.
Furthermore, in the fourth dhyāna, one should understand that there is a distinction characterized by the perception of defects in pleasure and by the complete purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
Herein, these are the synonyms for dhyāna, namely:
(2.4.1) Higher mind (*adhicitta*): because of correct meditative reflection (*samyagupanidhyāna*), having made the purification of the mind (*cittapariśuddhi*) the dominant influence.
(2.4.2) They are also called "abodes of happiness" (*sukhavihāra*), because in them one experiences complete happiness.

For in them, one experiences the happiness of joy (*prītisukha*), the happiness of tranquility (*prasrabdhisukha*), the happiness of equanimity (*upekṣāsukha*), and both physical and mental happiness.
Meditators, having repeatedly entered and emerged from these [attainments], experience them by way of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Therein, having entered, one experiences the dwelling in happiness in the present life that has become manifest.
Therein, having emerged, one experiences: "I have dwelt in such a state of happiness."
The formless attainments, however, are not experienced in that way;
therefore, they are not called "abodes of happiness."
Furthermore, having emerged from that state, they must be instructed.
For what reason?
Because there are indeed those who come to question a monk dwelling in the forest.
If a forest-dwelling monk, when questioned there on a point, does not provide an answer, then there will be those who say of him:

"What indeed is the use of this forest-dweller’s forest-dwelling, since now, when questioned on a matter concerning the peaceful liberations that transcend forms—the formless realms—he does not provide an answer!
Therefore, one should enter meditative attainments for the sake of explanation, not for the sake of dwelling.
H 66a6; C 331a17 (2.4.3) Furthermore, meditative absorption is called "nirvāṇa by way of its factors" (*tadaṅga-nirvāṇa*) and also "nirvāṇa by way of synonym" (*paryāya-nirvāṇa*).

It is called "nirvāṇa by way of its factors" because, through that factor, there is a partial abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*), yet [it is not definitive] because it is not a complete nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is "nirvāṇa by way of synonym."
In this regard, the four dhyānas are said to be the basis for the transcendence of feelings (*vedanā*).

Among them, the first dhyāna is the transcendence of mental distress (*daurmanasya*); the second is the transcendence of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*); the third is the transcendence of the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*); and the fourth is the transcendence of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*). Regarding equanimity (*upekṣā*), as stated by the Blessed One in the *Viparītaka-sūtra*:
In that regard, a monk understands as it truly is: "The faculty of mental distress has arisen.
In what state?
When he is engaged in its abandonment, he knows the continuum of consciousness being intermingled with the faculty of mental distress.
One understands, as it truly is, that this indeed has a cause, has conditions, has a source, has a specific form, and involves formative forces.
How does one understand it as having a cause?
By understanding the continuity of its seed.
How is it with its conditions (*sapratyaya*)? It discerns the basis not comprised within the seed, as well as the auxiliaries. How is it with its cause (*sanidāna*)?

Whatever object one relies upon for the arising of the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*), as well as its cause and the seed of ignorance that gives rise to that faculty of mental distress—
how is this "with aspect" (*sākāra*)?
He understands: "This has a miserable form.
How does it have conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*)?
He understands: "The volition associated with improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is its formative activity that brings it forth."
And having thus fully understood [this], he applies his mind toward deliverance. How does he apply it?
Having turned the mind away from afflicted activity, he applies it to the cultivation of mental attention (*manaskāra*).
That [affliction] is then ceased there without remainder until it reaches total exhaustion, both in terms of its latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and its active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
Therein, by means of mundane meditative absorption (*laukika-dhyāna*), he abandons the functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to that side, but he does not uproot its state as a seed.
For otherwise, by the extraction of that [defilement], there would be no further arising of it in the future.
Furthermore, one abandons both of those through the untainted (*anāsrava*) [path].
In the same way, this should be understood as applicable to the remaining cases according to their respective circumstances.
Furthermore, what kind of faculty of mental displeasure (*daurmanasyendriya*) does one fully understand?
He replied:
It is either afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or wholesome (*kuśala*) when accompanied by the desire for renunciation (*naiṣkramyacchanda*).

(2.4.4.1.3.2) The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) arises even for one free from passion (*vītarāga*), being governed by internal factors and so forth, or governed by physical exhaustion, or governed by fire-burns and the like, or governed by injuries inflicted by others. (2.4.4.1.3.3) The faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) in the second dhyāna belongs to the level of the second dhyāna.
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in the third dhyāna belongs to the level of the third dhyāna.
Why, then, is it said that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) has not been abandoned in the first dhyāna?
Because the corresponding coarseness (*dauṣṭhulya*) has not been abandoned there.
(2.4.4.1.4.2) For what reason does that [suffering] not manifest for one reborn in a dhyāna, even though it has not been abandoned?
Because of the abandonment of suffering comprised by the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*), which is its concomitant and counterpart.

(2.4.4.1.4.3) If, however, that faculty of suffering were abandoned even in the first dhyāna, then there would be no distinction here between a yogi who has entered the first dhyāna and one who has entered the second.
There would be no distinction between the meditative abidings (vihāra) based on feeling;
yet the dhyānas are said to be the escape from feeling,
since both possess joy and bliss.
Furthermore, by the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), no specific excellence in the abandonment of functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) would have been achieved for him.
In this same way, the subsequent abandonment of the other faculties should be understood as resulting from the abandonment of the functional rigidity associated with them.
Moreover, in this sutra, the Blessed One has taught the "signless" (*animitta*) as the signless mental concentration (*cetaḥsamādhi*).

Therein, the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) ceases without remainder—because of the eradication of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the associated dysfunctions (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to its side—but it does not cease there by way of active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*). Furthermore, in that state of the signless (*animitta*), there is necessarily the occurrence of all three—pleasure, mental joy, and equanimity;
yet there are no underlying tendencies for these faculties of feeling (*vedanendriya*).
Furthermore, that category of *dauṣṭhulya* (corruption) which is abandoned through the abandonment of a particular affliction is called the *anuśaya* (latent tendency) of those [afflictions].
Moreover, from what point until where is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) to be understood?
It extends from the fourth dhyāna up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).

H 67a2; C 331c1 (2.4.4.2.1.1) It should be understood that there is a mutual inclusion among these five faculties—which culminate in the signless (*animitta*)—and the five elements conducive to deliverance (*niḥsaraṇīya-dhātu*).
In this regard, by means of the deliverances from sensual desire, ill will, and harmfulness, the deliverance up to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is explained.
And by means of the deliverance from form, there is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) in the fourth dhyāna.
By the cessation of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya*), there is the cessation of the entire faculty of equanimity belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
What is the meaning of "conducive to deliverance" (*niḥsaraṇīya*)?
For one who abides in these [states] should be known as having emerged [from them]; therefore, they are called "conducive to deliverance."
However, liberation from them does not occur by means of those [three], because that realm is taught for those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*). (H 67a3;
C 331c8) When the abandonment of sensual desire, ill-will, and cruelty occurs at the very same time, for what reason is their liberation established separately?
Even though their liberation occurs simultaneously, there are three distinct designations for liberation due to the specific differences in the cultivation of their respective antidotes.
In this regard, the specific antidotes are as follows: respectively, the meditation on the foul, loving-kindness, and compassion.
Among these, some escape from all [afflictions] by cultivating the meditation on the foul, some by loving-kindness, and some by compassion.
For this very reason, a separate instruction on renunciation has been given.
Beyond that, however, the counteragent is of one and the same kind; thus, there is no further distinction above that point.
How does one with intense views recollect sensual pleasures?
He said:

"By means of the mental attention of investigation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-manaskāra*), through the mental attention directed toward the principal object, and through the mental attention of intense application. How does the mind not incline toward sensual pleasures?"
In that regard, it is from the perspective of not perceiving the benefits.
How does one fail to become serene?
It is because of the absence of the arising of delight and mental pleasure therein.
How does it not remain established?
In that regard, because of delighting in and finding pleasure in enjoyment.
How does it not resolve with conviction?

In that regard, how does one shrink back due to a lack of resolve regarding the grasping of signs through improper mental application (*ayoniśo-nimitta-grāha*)? It is when, being extended, it does not extend further.
How does it contract?
It abandons the grasped object.
How is it not extended?
Having applied discernment, when the mind is being held upon that object, it does not find delight.
How, then, does equanimity become established?
He is one who courses in an even state;
he directs his mind toward an even state.
What is disenchantment?
That which is aversion resulting from seeing the disadvantage therein is threefold:
by way of impermanence, suffering, and the nature of change.
What is disgust (*jugupsā*)? It is aversion resulting from the perception of the first [of the] defects (*ādīnava*). What is revulsion (*prativāni*)?
That which is aversion resulting from seeing the second disadvantage. What is aversion?
It is precisely that aversion which results from seeing the third disadvantage.
Furthermore, for one who attends to renunciation as the opposite of this [worldly state],
there is an "entry" because of seeing the benefits therein;
there is "clarity" because of the arising of faith, conviction, and serene confidence.
It becomes established through non-dispersal from that object.
It is liberated through dissociation from the afflictions by way of proceeding there without being defiled.
In this regard, for one who dwells in the modes of aversion and so forth, his mind becomes unimpeded; furthermore, in equanimity, it is effortless.
How does his mind become well-disposed toward the Sugata?
By being established in the mental attention that culminates in application (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*).
How does it become well-cultivated?
This is because other mental orientations have been well-cultivated.
By this, both the state of abandonment (*prahāṇāvasthā*) and the state of the path of application for abandonment (*prahāṇaprayogamārgāvasthā*) are indicated.

In that context, it is "liberated" (*mukta*) due to liberation from the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*); "freed" (*vimukta*) due to liberation from the signs of the object (*ālambananimitta*); and "thoroughly liberated" (*vipramukta*) due to liberation from the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Those outflows (*āsrava*) that arise for him conditioned by sensual desires— excluding the passion for sensual desire itself— are the other afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*).

The obstacles (*vighāta*) are those specific misdeeds, such as taking up weapons and so forth, which arise with those very [afflictions] as their cause, and through the performance and accumulation of which one is reborn in the miserable states (*apāya*).
Regarding "fever" (*paridāha*): because it has that as its cause, one who is consumed by craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatṛṣṇā*) is burned by both body and mind.
Regarding "distress" (*upāyāsa*): because it has that as its cause, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and distress arise from the transformation of those objects.

He is "liberated," "emerged," and "disjoined" from them—just as before—in the sense of liberation from the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), the objects (*ālambana*), and the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), respectively.
How is it that he does not experience feeling conditioned by those [objects]?
Because, whether desiring to perceive objects, perceiving them, or recollecting them, afflicted feeling does not arise through that basis;
his basis remains entirely unstained by afflictions, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.

H 67b4; C 332a20 (2.4.4.2.2) There are these six elements of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇīyā dhātavaḥ*). Furthermore, they have been cultivated by me exactly according to the Sūtra: "My loving-kindness (*maitrī*) has been cultivated, up to: 'the notion of "I am" (*asmīti*) has vanished from me'; yet nevertheless, the thorn of doubt and hesitation (*vicikitsākathaṃkathāśalya*) still remains, taking possession of my mind.

Therefore, this formal establishment of them should be understood as being for the purpose of abandoning the false grasping that "loving-kindness and the others are not the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to malice (*vyāpāda*) and so forth."

In that regard, the establishment of the four [concentrations] occurs through the distinction of their antidotes to aversion and so forth; the signless [concentration] is established by way of its being the antidote to signs and by way of the application of the examination for attaining the noble dwelling; and the sixth is established by way of the application of the examination for reaching the ultimate.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the antidote to ill-will (*vyāpāda*), because it proceeds from a state free of resentment.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is the antidote to cruelty (*vihiṃsā*), because it proceeds from the resolute intention to remove the suffering of others.
Joy (*muditā*) is the antidote to dissatisfaction (*arati*), because it proceeds in the form of rejoicing in the happiness of others.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the antidote to sensual desire and ill-will because it maintains indifference toward both.
The signless (*ānimitta*) is the antidote to all signs because it is diametrically opposed to signs.
Since there can be no possibility of doubt regarding one’s own liberation or realization for one who is free from the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), the absence of this conceit is its antidote.
One determines with certainty that "this is the escape from all ill-will," thinking:
"This is indeed the escape;
however, because [the mind] has not been cultivated, the fault of the manifestation of ill-will and so forth can still occur."

(2.4.4.2.3) Among those, of the five previous elements of deliverance (*niḥsaraṇīya-dhātu*), the first four are comprised within the divine abodes (*divyavihāra*), while the fifth is comprised within the noble abodes (*āryavihāra*).
Furthermore, among the six elements of deliverance, four are comprised within the sublime abodes (*brāhmavihāra*), while the fifth and sixth are indeed comprised within the noble abodes alone.
In this context, "deliverance" (*niḥsaraṇa*) refers to the transcendence of faults such as malice (*vyāpāda*).
H 68a1; C 332b7 (2.4.4.3.1) These are called "reliances" (*pratisaraṇa*) because they are to be relied upon for that deliverance.
Furthermore, four such reliances were taught by the Blessed One: "The Dharma is the reliance, not the person."
The meaning is the reliance, not the letter;
a sūtra of definitive meaning is the reliance, not one of interpretable meaning;
primordial wisdom is the reliance, not consciousness.
H 68a2; C 332b11 (2.4.4.3.2) How is their classification established?
It is by way of the distinction between four types of persons:

first, by the distinction of the person who is a pretender; second, by the distinction of the person who is a Lokāyatika; third, by the distinction of the person who persists in the adherence to their own views; and fourth, by the distinction of the person for whom learning is supreme.

In that regard, for one who is deceptive, the Dharma is the refuge, not the person, because it is to be realized through knowledge by means of the determination of discussion, and not by mere deportment alone.
Another formulation of this same point is: the Blessed One has taught both the person and the Dharma.
In this regard, the Dharma alone is the refuge, not the person, because of non-attachment to local dialects.
Furthermore, that Dharma is twofold: the letter and the meaning.
In this regard, the meaning is the reliance, not the letter;
for one should not be one for whom the heard is the ultimate, but rather the meaning should be reflected upon, weighed, and examined.
In that context, the Blessed One has taught both sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and those of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
In that regard, for one examining the meaning, a sūtra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) alone is the reliance, not one of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

In this context, the Blessed One has taught that even consciousness leading to merit or the imperturbable (*puṇyāneñjyopaga-vijñāna*) leads to a happy rebirth, and he has also taught knowledge regarding the four noble truths;
therein, for one practicing in accordance with the Dharma, knowledge is the reliance, not consciousness.
H 68a5; C 332b26 (2.4.4.3.4) In this regard, briefly stated, four persons are established on the basis of loss and non-loss during four periods:

at the time of acquiring the Dharma, at the time of retaining it, at the time of investigating its meaning, and at the time of practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma; and the four reliances are likewise established.
The systematic presentation is completed.
Furthermore, regarding these meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth, both the mental application (*manaskāra*) and the object of focus (*ālambana*) are to be understood.
Among these, there are seven fundamental mental applications and forty other mental applications.
H 68a6; C 332c3 (3.1.1) What are the seven mental orientations (*manaskāra*)?

They are as follows: the mental orientation of perceiving characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*), that of resolute conviction (*ādhimokṣika*), that of seclusion (*prāvivekya*), that which gathers delight (*ratisaṃgrāhaka*), the mental orientation of investigation (*mīmāṃsāmanaskāra*), the mental orientation of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭha*), and the mental orientation of the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*).
H 68a6; C 332c5 (3.1.2.1) What are the forty mental orientations?
Attention directed toward phenomena (*dharmamanasikāra*), attention directed toward meaning (*arthamanasikāra*);
attention having the body as its object, and attention having feeling, mind, and phenomena as its objects;
attention consisting of resolute belief (*adhimuktimanaskāra*), and attention consisting of reality (*tattvamanaskāra*).
The one in training (śaikṣa), the one beyond training (aśaikṣa), and the one who is neither in training nor beyond training;

the mental attention of thorough knowledge (parijñā-manasikāra), the mental attention of abandonment (prahāṇa-manasikāra), and the mental attention regarding what has been abandoned (prahīṇe manaskāra);

that which has a conceptual image as its object (savikalpa-pratibimba-ālambana), that which has a non-conceptual image as its object (nirvikalpa-pratibimba-ālambana), that which has the limit of phenomena as its object (vastu-paryanta-ālambana), and that which has the fulfillment of the task as its object (kārya-pariniṣpatti-ālambana).

Mental application consisting of the investigation of resolute belief; that which leads to tranquility; cultivated in one part; cultivated in both parts; continuous mental application; respectful mental application; conformable; counteractive;
inspiring confidence; conducive to discernment; forceful operation; interrupted operation; effortful operation; and spontaneous operation.

The mental application of investigation (*vicaya-manaskāra*), the internally concentrated (*adhyātma-saṃpiṇḍita*), the purification of hindrances (*āvaraṇa-viśodhana*), the purity of the sphere of the perfected basis (*āśraya-niṣpatti-gocara-viśuddha*);
the mental application brought about by others (*parapraṇīta*), the internal realization (*pratyātma-adhigraha*), the sublime (*udāra*), and the all-pervading (*sarvatraga*) mental application.
(H 68b2; C 332c19) In that regard, what is the mental application having phenomena as its object (*dharma-ālambana*)?
That which is associated with wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*).
(H 68b2; C 332c19) That which has meaning as its object (*arthālambana*) and is associated with wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*) and wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*).

(H 68b2; C 332c20) That which has the body as its object, up to that which has phenomena (*dharma*) as its object—the mental attention (*manaskāra*) of one engaged in the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), who is correctly attending (*yoniśo manasikurvat*) to the body and so forth.
(3.1.2.2.7) Attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manaskāra*) is that by which meditators resolve upon a sign or object according to their wish.

(3.1.2.2.8) Attention to reality (*tattva-manaskāra*) is the attention of one who correctly attends to phenomena (*dharmas*) by way of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
(3.1.2.2.9) The learner (*śaikṣa*) is of two kinds:
By way of intrinsic nature and by way of continuity.
Therein, that which is by way of intrinsic nature is the untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manaskāra*) of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
That which is by way of continuity is all wholesome mental attention whatsoever belonging to one in training.

(3.1.2.2.10) Just as it is with the one in training (*śaikṣa*), so too should the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) be understood as being twofold. (3.1.2.2.11) That which is neither in training nor beyond training is all mundane mental attention (*laukika-manaskāra*).
(3.1.2.2.12) Mental attention consisting of full comprehension (*parijñā-manaskāra*) is that by which one fully comprehends the object of focus, but does not yet abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*).
(3.1.2.2.13) The attention of abandonment (*prahāṇamanaskāra*) is that by which one performs both [tasks].
(3.1.2.2.14) The attention regarding what has been abandoned (*prahīṇe manaskāra*) is the subsequent attention directed toward those afflictions (*kleśa*) that have already been abandoned.

(3.1.2.2.15) The attention having a conceptual image as its object (*savikalpapratibimbālambano manaskāraḥ*) is that by which one cultivates insight (*vipaśyanā*) that takes the conceptual body as its object.
(3.1.2.2.16) That which has a non-conceptual reflection as its object is that by means of which one cultivates calm abiding (*śamatha*) having a conceptual body as its object.

(3.1.2.2.17) That which has the limit of phenomena (*vastuparyanta*) as its object is that by means of which one takes as its object the limits of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena regarding the body and so forth, [thinking]:
“Beyond this there is no further body,” up to “there are no further phenomena.”

(3.1.2.2.18) Mental attention having the accomplishment of the task as its object is that which thinks: “As I attend to this, as I attend in this way, this and that will come to be; this and that will be accomplished. And there is that which has the object of complete purity as its object. (3.1.2.2.19) Mental attention consisting of resolve and investigation is that by means of which one first investigates the phenomena, or does so preceded by calm abiding (*śamatha*).
(3.1.2.2.20) The attention that is pacifying (*aupaśamika*) is that which, for one who is first establishing the mind internally, either precedes or is preceded by insight (*vipaśyanā*).

(3.1.2.2.21) The attention cultivated in one part (*ekāṃśabhāvita*) is that by which one cultivates either calm (*śamatha*) or insight in one part. (3.1.2.2.22) The attention cultivated in both parts (*ubhayāṃśabhāvita*) is that by which one cultivates both in equal union.
(3.1.2.2.23) Constant mental attention (*sātatyamanasikāra*) is that which occurs at all times, flowing without interruption or gap.
(3.1.2.2.24) Respectful mental attention (*satkṛtyamanasikāra*) is that which is characterized by non-lax application.

(3.1.2.2.ad19–24) Therein, through the mental attention that investigates resolute belief (*adhimukti-vicaya-manasikāra*), one purifies knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*); through that which is conducive to tranquility (*aupaśamika*), one generates pliancy (*prasrabdhi*).
By means of that which is cultivated in one part and that which is cultivated in both parts, he liberates the mind from the hindrances;
by means of continuous mental attention, he makes his time not in vain;
and by means of respectful mental attention, he attains swift direct knowledge.
(3.1.2.2.25) Conforming attention (*anulomika-manaskāra*) is that which is conducive to the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*), by means of which one reviles the object of focus (*ālambana*).
(3.1.2.2.26) Counteractive attention (*prātipakṣika*) is that by which one abandons the afflictions, maintains that abandonment, and distances the continuum (*saṃtati*) from the afflictions.
(3.1.2.2.27) Clarifying attention (*prasadanīya-manaskāra*) is that of one who cultivates the six recollections (*anusmṛti*), or who attends to any other clarifying object.

(3.1.2.2.28) That which is to be examined (*pratyavekṣaṇīya*) is that by means of which one thoroughly investigates whether afflictions have been abandoned or not abandoned, or examines one’s own realization, or [examines] those phenomena previously investigated. (3.1.2.2.29) That which operates with effort (*balavāhana*) is that of beginners who have not yet attained mental attention (*manaskāra*).
(3.1.2.2.30) That which carries with interruptions is that of those who have attained mental attention but whose application subsequently becomes lax.

(3.1.2.2.31) That which carries with effort is that of those very same individuals when they have initiated vigor and their application is not lax. (3.1.2.2.32) That which carries by its own natural flow is that which is fixed at four times:

At the time of attaining mental attention (*manaskāra*), at the time of the fundamental meditative attainments (*maulasamāpatti*) and for those who have entered them, at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), and at the time of attaining and having attained arhatship.
(3.1.2.2.33) Discerning mental attention (*vicayamanaskāra*) is that which belongs to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
(3.1.2.2.34) Internally concentrated mental attention (*adhyātmasaṃpiṇḍita*) is that which belongs to the side of calm (*śamatha*).

(3.1.2.2.35) That which purifies obstructions (*āvaraṇaviśodhana*) is that by which one abandons the outflows (*āsrava*) and eradicates the state of corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*). (3.1.2.2.36) That which is purified in its objective field through the perfection of the basis (*āśrayaniṣpattigocaraviśuddha*) is that by which the basis, being free from all corruption, no longer gives rise to afflictions (*kleśa*) even while operating upon an object of perception (*ālambana*).

(3.1.2.2.37) That which is brought about by another (*parapraṇīta*) is, for example, that of the Śrāvakas, which arises from hearing the voice of another and from appropriate mental attention (*yoniśomanaskāra*) within oneself.
(3.1.2.2.38) Individual realization (*pratyātmādhigama*) is, for example, that of the *pratyekabuddhas* and *bodhisattvas*, because they attain perfect awakening without a teacher.

(3.1.2.2.39) Sublime mental attention (*udāro manaskāraḥ*) is, for example, that of the *bodhisattvas* who possess knowledge of the faults of *saṃsāra* and the means of escape from them, and who are intent upon the vow for awakening (*bodhipraṇidhāna*).

(3.1.2.2.40) Pervasive mental attention (*sarvatraga manaskāraḥ*) is, for example, that of the Blessed Buddhas, which is associated with omniscient knowledge that is non-obscured and non-erroneous regarding all things, as well as that of the *bodhisattvas*.
And for those practicing skill in the three vehicles or, alternatively, in the five fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*).
Among these, the attention consisting of the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) has both the teachings (*dharma*) and their meaning (*artha*) as its objects;
however, the other six types of attention have only the meaning as their object.
Mental orientations (manaskāra) that have the body and so forth as their objects are to be understood as occurring in all seven [stages].

The mental orientation of discerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*), the mental orientation of resolute conviction (*ādhimokṣika*), and the mental orientation of the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*) are subsumed under the mental orientations of conviction (*adhimukti*) and reality (*tattva*).
The mental orientation of investigation (*mīmāṃsāmanaskāra*) is subsumed under the mental orientation of conviction alone.
The remaining three are exclusively mental applications directed toward reality (*tattvamanaskāra*), based on the preceding formulation.
However, they should be understood by others according to their respective application.
All seven are [the states] of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
There are two types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*):
the one who experiences the characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedin*), which belongs to the pure stage (*śuddhabhūmika*), and the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*).

The experience of characteristics, the mental engagement of resolute conviction (*ādhimokṣika*), and the mental engagement of investigation (*mīmāṃsāmanaskāra*) are the mental engagements of thorough knowledge (*parijñāmanaskāra*).
The remaining three are the mental applications of abandonment (*prahāṇa-manaskāra*);
the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala*) occurs when [the afflictions] have been abandoned.

H 69b2; C 333b29 (3.1.3.ad15–18). The mental application of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manaskāra*) has as its object only a conceptualized reflection (*savikalpa-pratibimba*); the remaining ones are of both kinds.
All [mental applications] have the limit of things (*vastuparyanta*) as their object.

Regarding those that have the accomplishment of the task (*kāryapariniṣpatti*) as their object: according to the first formulation, all [mental applications] are included; according to the second, only the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*) is included.

As for the mental application of discernment through resolute belief (*adhimuktivicayamanaskāra*): that which is the very first is not included [in the category of the fruit], whereas that which is preceded by calm abiding (*śamatha*) is included in all [the categories].

In this way, the first [type of] calming preceded by insight should be understood. Six [types of cultivation] are cultivated through both parts; the fruit of the culmination of application is cultivated through both parts alone. Constant attention and respectful attention apply to all of them.

The conformable [mental application] is subsumed by the first two; the counteractive is subsumed by the [stages of] seclusion and the culmination of application; the gladdening is a portion of the joy-inducing [mental application] itself;
and the mental application of investigation is subsumed solely by the mental application of examining abandonment and non-abandonment.
This has been stated after concluding the discussion on the counteragent of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*);
however, the others should be understood according to their respective applications.
[The path] that proceeds with effort (*balavāhana*) is not [counteracted] by anything.

The [mental application] with interruptions and with effortful engagement lasts as long as the mental application that gathers delight (*ratisaṃgrāhaka*). The [mental application] flowing by its own natural force (*svarasavāhana*) consists of the mental application at the culmination of practice (*prayoganiṣṭha*) and its fruit (*tatphala*).
The mental application of investigation (*vicaya*) consists of the mental application of discerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*).
That which is inwardly concentrated is comprised by the stage of resolute belief.
That which purifies hindrances is comprised by the stages of seclusion, delight, gathering, investigation, application, and culmination.
That which results in the perfection of the basis and the purity of the objective sphere is comprised solely by the fruit of the culmination of application.
It is established by others and personally realized by all.
It is sublime and not [established] by anyone. It is omnipresent; that which is first is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*).
The second, however, is [accomplished] by all [factors].

For the [knowledge] that experiences the characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedin*), if it is brought about by another, then the external voice and internal wise attention (*yoniśomanaskāra*) are its cause for one who is concentrated;
if, on the other hand, it is an internal realization, then its cause is precisely the prior accumulation of merit and knowledge.
For the remaining [factors], the preceding one is the cause of the succeeding one.
H 69b6; C 333c25 (3.2.0) What is the object of focus (*ālambana*)?
It is the sign (*nimitta*).
H 69b6; C 333c25 (3.2.1.0) What is the sign (*nimitta*)?
In brief, it should be understood as fourfold:
the sign of the object (*ālambananimitta*), the sign of the cause (*nidānanimitta*), the sign to be avoided (*parivarjanīya*), and the sign to be cultivated (*pratiniṣevaṇīya*).
(3.2.1.1) What is the sign of the object (*ālambananimitta*)?
It is the conceptual body (*vikalpaśarīra*) of the knowable thing (*jñeya*).
(3.2.1.2) What is the causal sign (*nidānanimitta*)?
That which is the equipment for meditative concentration (*samādhi-sambhāra*).
What is the sign (*nimitta*) to be avoided?
It is fourfold:
The sign of lethargy, the sign of restlessness, the sign of distraction, and the sign of attachment.
What is the sign to be cultivated?
It should be understood as the antidote to those [four].

(3.2.1.3B.1) What is the sign of indolence (*layanimitta*)? It consists of: not guarding the doors of the sense faculties, lack of moderation in eating, failure to apply oneself to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, dwelling without clear comprehension, behaving with delusion, being fond of sleep, lack of knowledge of skillful means, desire, vigor, mind, and investigation accompanied by laziness, lack of cultivation of tranquility (*śamatha*), one-sided mental attention to tranquility by one who has not mastered tranquility, and appearing as if shrouded in darkness.
And the mind’s lack of inclination toward the object of focus. H 70a3; C 334a6 (3.2.1.3B.2) What is the cause of restlessness?

It consists of the four factors previously mentioned, beginning with not guarding the doors of the sense faculties; being of a lustful temperament; having a nature that lacks tranquility; having a mind that is not agitated by a sense of urgency; lacking knowledge of the proper means; and having zeal and so forth accompanied by excessive excitation.

As before, there is the non-cultivation of *pragraha* (exertion); for one who has not mastered *pragraha*, there is the cultivation of it in only a single aspect; and there is the distraction of the mind by any one of the factors conducive to agitation, such as thoughts of kin (*jñātivitarka*) and so forth. What is the cause of distraction? It consists of the four [factors] beginning with not guarding the doors of the sense faculties, as described before; being of a discursive temperament (*vitarkacarita*); having dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*); having many concerns, many duties, and many occupations; having an unconcerned mind (*asaṃvignacitta*); and lack of knowledge regarding skillful means (*anupāyajñatā*).

Lack of practice in solitude, lack of inclination toward the focal object, creating gaps in application due to social contact, and lack of attentiveness regarding the thorough knowledge of distraction and non-distraction.
What is the sign of attachment (*saṅganimitta*)?

It consists of the four factors beginning with not guarding the doors of the sense faculties, as previously described; moreover, it includes having dull faculties, being dominated by craving, abundance of afflictions, improper mental attention, failure to see the disadvantages [of worldly things], and failing to see the higher transcendence.
H 70a5; C 334a17 (3.2.1.4B) It should be understood that, as an antidote to those [factors] to be avoided, there are corresponding factors to be practiced.
H 70a6; C 334a20 (3.2.2.1) There are another thirty-two signs (*nimitta*):

the sign of one's own mind, the sign of the external, the sign of the basis (*āśraya*), the sign of the objective sphere (*gocara*), the sign of mental attention (*manaskāra*), the sign of the arising of the mind, the sign of its stability, and the sign of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

The sign of general characteristics, the coarse sign, the sign of tranquility, the sign of experience, the sign of conceptualization, that which accompanies [the mind], the afflicted sign, the unafflicted sign,

the sign of correct application, the sign of false application, the sign of light, the sign of investigation, the auspicious sign of meditative concentration, the sign of calm abiding, and the sign of exertion.

The sign of insight (*vipaśyanā-nimitta*), the sign of equanimity (*upekṣā-nimitta*), the sign of concentration (*samādhi-nimitta*), the sign of the stability of concentration (*samādhi-sthiti-nimitta*), the sign of emergence from concentration (*samādhi-vyutthāna-nimitta*), the sign of coming (*āya-nimitta*), the sign of going (*apāya-nimitta*), the sign of means (*upāya-nimitta*), and the sign of accomplishment (*abhinirhāra-nimitta*).
(3.2.2.2.1) What is the sign of one’s own mind (*svacitta-nimitta*)?
In this case, a monk, prior to the defilement of the mind, correctly and thoroughly grasps the sign within his own mind:
"In such and such a way the mind becomes defiled or does not become defiled.
He understands: "This is the means for [remedying] mental sinking and so forth; this is for the four [states] beginning with non-sinking," up to "for the non-attachment of the mind."
Furthermore, regarding a defiled mind:
what is the external sign (*bahirdhānimitta*)?
It is as follows: when the mind is defiled, having recognized, "My mind is defiled," one apprehends an external sign for the purpose of removing that very defilement and ensuring it does not recur.
That is to say: the sign of light, or that which is inspiring, or whatever else there may be.
(H 70b3; C 334b5) What is the sign of the basis (*āśrayanimitta*)?
It is the conceptual body of all the five aggregates, together with their seeds, which are included within one's own personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
(3.2.2.2.4) What is the sign of the objective field (*gocaranimitta*)?
It is when one attends to the conceptual body of whichever object, from form (*rūpa*) up to mental phenomena (*dharma*).
(3.2.2.2.5) What is the sign of attention (*manasikāranimitta*)?
When there is the corresponding attention (*manaskāra*), the arising of the corresponding consciousness occurs in each respective object.
For one who attends thus: "Indeed, this mind of mine proceeds toward its object through attention, not without attention"—that is the sign (*nimitta*).
What is the sign for the arising of the mind?
This very point just mentioned is the first;
the second is the sign for one who attends to the mind as being "conditioned by formative forces" (*saṃskāra*) and "conditioned by name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
What is the sign of stability (*sthitinimitta*)?
The four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*):
the sign of one who attends in detail according to the sūtra, thinking, "consciousness abides accompanied by form," and so forth.
(H 70b5; C 334b14) What is the sign of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇanimitta*)?
The sign for one who attends to either the characteristic of its own class (*svajātilakṣaṇa*) or the individual characteristic (*pratyekalakṣaṇa*).
(H 70b6; C 334b16) What is the sign of the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇanimitta*)?

It is the sign for one who attends to either the general characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the general characteristic of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*), or the general characteristic of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
(3.2.2.2.10) What is the coarse sign (*audārikanimitta*)? It is the sign for one who views a lower stage as coarse.
(3.2.2.2.11) What is the sign of peace (*śāntanimitta*)?
The sign for one who contemplates the higher stages as peaceful.
(H 71a1; C 334b19) What is the sign of experience?
It is the sign for one who recollects past conditioned phenomena previously experienced.
(3.2.2.2.13) What is the sign of conceptualization (*vikalpanimitta*)?
It is the sign of one who conceptualizes future conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
(3.2.2.2.14) What is the concomitant sign (*sahānucaranimitta*)?
The sign for one who attends to present conditioned phenomena.
(H 71a1; C 334b22) What is the defiled sign?
It is the sign for one who attends to a mind with lust as "a mind with lust," and so on in detail, up to attending to a mind that is not well-liberated as "a mind that is not well-liberated."
(3.2.2.2.16) What is the non-afflicted sign (*akliṣṭanimitta*)? It should be understood that the non-afflicted sign is the opposite of this [afflicted sign].

(3.2.2.2.ad15–16) In that regard, the contemplation of [the mind] as being with passion and so forth pertains to those who have departed [from the world] but are not engaged in the application for abandonment.
For those who have applied themselves [to meditation], there is the examination of states such as the contracted or the sunken.
In that regard, "with passion" refers to that which is associated with passion, or that which is accompanied by the functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to its side.

In this way, all afflicted minds should be understood according to their respective cases in terms of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); alternatively, they are non-afflicted when they serve as the antidote to the outbursts and latent tendencies.

(3.2.2.2.17) What is the sign of correct application (*samyakprayoga-nimitta*)? It is the sign that arises for one who attends to the causal sign belonging to the white side (*śuklapakṣika*). (3.2.2.2.18) What is the sign of false application (*mithyāprayoga-nimitta*)?
The sign for one who attends to the causal basis (*nidāna*) belonging to the dark side;
the sign for one who attends to it thus: “In this way and that way the mind becomes defiled for one who dwells with the doors of the senses unguarded, up to dwelling without clear comprehension.
What is the sign of light (*ālokanimitta*)?

For example, here a certain person has properly and thoroughly grasped the sign from the light of the Dharma that is the antidote to darkness, and has well attended to it—just as [it is] below, so too above.
This is established as the antidote to the sign of darkness.
What is the sign of analytical observation (*pratyavekṣaṇānimitta*)?

In this case, a monk has properly and thoroughly grasped the sign of contemplation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-nimitta*) as follows: "standing, he contemplates one who is sitting"—this is the contemplation of future objects of apprehension by means of a present subject of apprehension.
Or, "sitting, [he contemplates] one who is lying down"—this is the contemplation of past objects of apprehension by means of a present subject of apprehension itself.
Or, "walking behind, he contemplates one walking in front"—this is the contemplation of a preceding subject of apprehension by means of a subsequent subject of apprehension.
Thus, this analytical investigation of the phenomena of the grasped and the grasper has been briefly explained as being twofold.

What is the favorable sign of meditative concentration (*samādhinimitta*)? It is the sign that arises for one who attends to the livid corpse (*vinīlaka*) and so forth, serving as the antidote to sensual desire.
Why is this called "auspicious"?
Because passion (*rāga*) is the primary among all afflictions (*kleśa*), and among all forms of passion, sensual passion (*kāmarāga*) is that which must be eradicated along with all suffering;
and this [meditation] is its antidote as an object of focus (*ālambana*).
Therefore, it is called "auspicious.
What is the sign of calm abiding (*śamatha-nimitta*)? It is the sign for one who is attending to a non-conceptual mental image.
(3.2.2.2.23) What is the sign of exertion (*pragrahanimitta*)? It is the sign for one who exerts the mind by means of any one of the inspiring [objects] or the sign of light.
(3.2.2.2.24) What is the sign of insight (*vipaśyanānimitta*)?
The sign for one who attends to phenomena with the wisdom consisting of hearing, the wisdom consisting of reflection, and the wisdom consisting of cultivation.
(H 71b1; C 334c20, 3.2.2.2.25) What is the sign of equanimity?
It is the sign for one who, while the mind has attained equilibrium, maintains equanimity toward the side of the wholesome.

(3.2.2.2.26) What is the sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*)? It refers to those signs—consisting of causes and objects of focus that are to be cultivated—by means of which one enters into concentration, or brings back into manifestation a concentration already attained. (3.2.2.2.27) What is the sign for the stability of concentration (*samādhisthitinimitta*)?
It is the thorough grasping of those very signs; because of that thorough grasping, he remains in meditative attainment for as long as he desires;
and it consists of those qualities which do not lead to the decline of that concentration.
H 71b2; C 334c25 (3.2.2.2.28) What is the sign of emergence from meditative concentration (*samādhivyutthānanimitta*)?
It is that which belongs to the level of non-concentration and is not comprised within the body of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
H 71b2; C 334c26 (3.2.2.2.29) What is the sign of coming (*āyanimitta*)?

The sign for one who attends to the further increase, growth, and expansion of the concentration already attained. (H 71b2; C 334c27, 3.2.2.2.30) What is the sign of decline? It is the sign for one who attends to the loss, diminution, and attenuation of the concentration already attained.
What is the sign of acquisition?
It is the path pertaining to both [the wholesome and the unwholesome],
for the purpose of attaining further increase, growth, and expansion, or for the purpose of decline.
(3.2.2.2.32) What is the sign of actualization (*abhinirhāranimitta*)?

It is the sign that arises when one condenses the meaning of extensive words and phrases; or when one actualizes the superknowledges (*abhijñā*); or when, by relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one realizes through wisdom a profound word of meaning—whether it be the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), or other distinguished qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*). This is the sign.
Furthermore, all these signs are subsumed under four fundamental signs:
by the sign of the object (*ālambananimitta*), which includes them all;
and by the sign of the cause (*nidānanimitta*), because the preceding [sign] is the cause for the subsequent one, leading to a progressive increasing clarity.
Right application, however, is in every respect the very cause of the [true] motive.
Just as right application is, so too is wrong application;
the former belongs to the white side (śuklapakṣa), while the second belongs to the black side (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
In that regard, every afflicted sign (*nimitta*) is to be completely abandoned.
It should be understood that the other [signs] are to be cultivated at their respective times.
(H 71b5; C 335a15, 3.2.4) In this context, how does one cultivate mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward the signs of the object (*ālambana-nimitta*)?
Whatever sign one brings to mind, while bringing it to mind, one performs four tasks:

one cultivates that very mental attention; one distances oneself from the afflictions that are its opposite; one heats up that very mental attention or something else, namely for the sake of its arising in the future in an even more refined state;
and while cultivating that mental attention, one reviles the object, abandons the affliction, maintains the abandonment, and distances the continuum from the afflictions.
In this way, one cultivates mental attention that takes signs as its object.
One enters the first dhyāna, and so on up to the peak of existence, by means of four causes:
the power of the cause, the power of application, the power of the objective, and the power of instruction.
(3.3.1.1) How is it by the power of the cause? One has entered a meditative absorption that is close to being attained.
(3.3.1.2) How is it by the power of application?
Even one who has not attained [the meditative absorption] in proximity, by frequently entering it through the power of constant practice, [attains it].

How [does one attain it] by the power of the summary (*uddeśabala*)? It is as explained in detail: "By him many dharmas governed by the meditative absorptions have been heard and retained," and so forth.
Relying on those very same dharmas, dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, practicing in accordance with the Dharma, he enters into meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
How [does this occur] through the power of instruction?

From a teacher, or a preceptor, or from one or another who occupies the position of a guru, he receives the preliminary advice and instruction conducive to the first meditative absorption, and likewise for the remaining [absorptions].
Directing his attention precisely toward that [object], he enters meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
These four types of practitioners are: one who possesses the power of the cause, one who possesses the power of application, one with sharp faculties, and one with dull faculties.
There are these four meditators:

One who meditates with craving as the dominant factor, one who meditates with views as the dominant factor, one who meditates with pride as the dominant factor, and one who meditates with doubt as the dominant factor. (H 72a2;

C 335b9) What is one who meditates with craving as the dominant factor? It is one by whom the benefit of the attainment of meditation has already been heard previously, but the escape from it has not been heard.
Therein, perceiving the benefit through one aspect, he enters the first dhyāna by means of ardent application; having thus entered it, he subsequently relishes it.
What is the one who practices meditation based on views (*dṛṣṭyuttaradhyāyin*)?

In this case, someone has heard from his own teacher or from another that "the world is eternal," and so forth, or that "one is purified and liberated in this way; in this way one attains the first dhyāna, up to the peak of existence."
Relying on that very view and through diligent application, he enters the first dhyāna;
having thus attained it, he recollects his former existences for many eons.
It occurs to him:
“The self and the world are eternal. Having emerged from that concentration, he strengthens that very view and subsequently meditates, ponders, and reflects upon it:
“By this I shall be purified, I shall be liberated, I shall go forth [to salvation].”
H 72a4; C 335b21 (3.4.3) Who is the one who meditates with pride as his superior?
It is when someone here has heard:
“The venerable one named so-and-so enters the first dhyāna, up to the peak of existence.”
And having heard this, it occurs to him:
"If even he attains that,
why should I not attain it?"
Relying on that conceit and through the application of diligent effort, he enters the first dhyāna; having thus entered it, he becomes elated by it.
Or, while having entered it, it occurs to him as follows:
