“I am one who has attained the first meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samāpatti*), whereas others have not. Relying on that very conceit (*māna*), he further meditates, contemplates, and reflects [with pride].
(H 72a5; C 335b28) Who is the one who meditates with doubt (*vicikitsottara-dhyāyin*)?
It is like someone here who is by nature dull-witted and deluded.
He is one who previously practiced tranquility (*śamatha*); therefore, he enters into meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
Having thus entered it, he exerts himself further for the attainment of what has not yet been attained, for the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the four noble truths.
Due to his dullness and delusion, he is unable to effect the direct realization of the truths.
In him, a longing for the attainment of others also arises, and doubt arises.
Relying upon that longing, he further meditates, contemplates, and reflects.
How does one enter a dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādana*)?
He has dull faculties and is either dominated by passion or characterized by an abundance of afflictions.
He hears in detail the benefits of attaining the first dhyāna, just as one who meditates with craving [hears the benefits].
Not knowing the higher escape, he relishes it, approves of it, becomes intent upon it, and having become intent, he remains fixed therein.
That which one relishes, from that one must be said to have emerged; that by which one relishes, that is what one has attained. How does one attain pure (*śuddhaka*) dhyāna?
He may be of middling faculties or sharp faculties; he may have moderate afflictions or few passions.

Having heard from another about the gratification and the danger of the attainment of the first dhyāna, as well as the escape from it in the higher [stages], he enters the first dhyāna through the application of diligent effort.
Having entered [the meditative attainment], while attending to that very disadvantage and further discerning the escape, he does not relish it.
How does one enter untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyāna?
It is when someone here is either a follower by faith (*śraddhānusārī*) or a follower of the Dharma (*dharmānusārī*), being of a nature with dull defilements (*mandarajaska*).
By him, the four noble truths have already been realized, or he is engaged in their realization.
With whatever aspects, marks, and signs he enters the first dhyāna, he does not attend to those aspects, marks, or signs;

rather, whatever exists therein—whether belonging to the category of form or up to the category of consciousness—he attends to those phenomena with aspects such as being a disease and so forth, and thereby causes his mind to become weary of, terrified of, and turns away from those conditioned formations.
And he brings [the mind] into rest within the deathless element (*amṛtadhātu*).
In this way, he enters the untainted (*anāsrava*) state.
(H 72b3; C 335c23) How does he enter that which pertains to decline (*hānabhāgīya*)?
He possesses dull faculties and inferior resolve.
As he enters the first dhyāna through the application of effort, being unable to endure the joy, the bliss, and the benefit therein, he falls away from that dhyāna.
To whatever extent he enters it, to that same extent he falls away, until he sharpens his faculties.

(3.5.2.2) How does one attain the meditative attainment conducive to stability (*sthitibhāgīya*)? One who possesses either medium faculties or sharp faculties hears of its benefits in detail, as previously described in connection with the relishing (*āsvādana*) [of the dhyāna].
Relishing that [attainment], he neither transcends it further nor falls away from it below.
How does one enter the attainment conducive to distinction (*viśeṣabhāgīya*)?
He has heard of the escape from this [state] by means of that [attainment].
Because he is not satisfied with that attainment, he does not relish it and strives for what is higher;
thus, he attains distinction.
How does he enter the attainments conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)?
Everywhere he perceives the danger in the view of a self-identity (*satkāya*).
Thereupon, he enters the untainted state (*anāsrava*).
And all that is untainted is called "conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), because it reaches the ultimate limit.
Just as it is said that a gem is "pierced," a jar is "pierced," or a hide is "pierced"—
and because there is no further piercing beyond that point, it is called "pierced"—
in the same way, because there is no further penetration beyond it, it is called "conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
H 72b6; C 336a9 (3.5.3) How does one enter [the meditative attainments] without interruption?
It is when a certain person here becomes an attainer of the first dhyāna that is impure and unpurified, up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
He enters the meditative attainments in successive order and in reverse order, from the peak of existence down to the first dhyāna.
(3.5.4) How does one enter the leaping meditative attainments (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*)?
Because those [stages] are thoroughly purified, immediately after the first dhyāna, one enters the third;
from there, one proceeds as far as the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Then there is the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). There is no leaping meditation (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*) beyond the third [sphere] because it is too remote.
The same applies in reverse order as well.
Setting aside the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattva who has emerged after two incalculable eons— because for those two, meditative attainments arise according to their will—
how do they intermingle the dhyānas?
It is when a certain person becomes a possessor of both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) four dhyānas.
He either desires to attain mastery over meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) or desires to experience the fruit of mastery over meditative attainment.

He enters into a continuous flow of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), alternating between them, until—immediately after the contaminated, there is the uncontaminated; immediately after the uncontaminated, there is the contaminated.
To this extent, its perfection should be understood.
"Wherever, whenever, and for as long as he desires, there, then, and for that long, he enters meditative absorption.
This is mastery over meditative absorption (*samāpattivaśitā*). Furthermore, the fruit of mastery over meditative absorption is as follows:

His dwelling in happiness in the present life becomes more radiant, and he has attained a path from which there is no falling away; furthermore, the path for the realization of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) is purified. If he passes away while still possessing a remainder of substrate (*sopadhiśeṣa*), he then enters the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.

H 73a3; C 336a29 (3.6.2.2) Through the distinction of weak, medium, and intense meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*), there are in every case three levels as previously described, namely, as in the level with applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*).
By cultivating a concentration that is without applied thought and consists of sustained thought alone (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), the state of Mahābrahmā is attained. H 73a3;

C 336b2 (3.6.2.3) Due to being cultivated weakly, moderately, intensely, more intensely, and most intensely—having been cultivated in a mixed manner—the five levels of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) have come into existence.

In this regard, it should be understood that rebirth in the stages of dhyāna occurs through the attainment of pure (*śuddhaka*) dhyāna, and not through that which is associated with relishing (*āsvādana*).
Furthermore, if one who has been reborn there should relish [the state], he falls away from it;
but if he cultivates the pure [dhyāna], he is reborn in that very same place or in a lower one.
Or, having attained a higher [meditative state], one migrates upward.
Here first there is the meditative attainment, and subsequently there is rebirth there.
For what reason?
One who is not free from passion is not reborn there;
nor is there detachment for an ordinary person who has not attained meditative absorption.
Furthermore, no specific excellence of bliss exists for those who have attained absorption, whether here or there.
However, a distinction regarding the basis does exist.
C 336b11) (3.Ω) The cultivation of the signs of mental attention is completed.
What is the compendium of the sūtras?
It consists of the eight liberations, beginning with "one possessing form sees forms," as previously described.
Because one who is liberated is resolved [upon these], there are thus seven liberations.
The eight liberations are spoken of by way of turning away from perception and feeling.
How does one who possesses form see forms?
Born and existing in the desire realm, one attains detachment from the desire realm but not yet detachment from the realm of form.
Thus liberated, he brings to mind and resolves upon those very forms belonging to the desire realm from which he is liberated, by means of the sign of luminous light.

He becomes possessed of form for two reasons: because he was born and has existed in the desire realm, and because he has attained the meditative absorption of the form realm; furthermore, he resolves upon them as being radiant.
Regarding the statement "he sees forms," what kind of forms does he see,
and for what reason?

Having broken through the forms belonging to the desire realm, those which have been cultivated in the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)—whether limited or extensive, beautiful or ugly, inferior or superior—and likewise those that are excessive:
for what reason?

For the sake of the preparatory refinement of the application in order to bring forth distinguished qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*), such as the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), as well as noble supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and so forth.

Even though he has previously been free from passion (*vītarāga*) regarding those forms, he has not yet attained mastery over resolve (*adhimukti-vaśitā*) with respect to them; therefore, for the sake of attaining that, he resolves upon them again and again.
(4.1.1.1.2) How is it that one who is internally without the perception of form (*arūpa-saṃjñin*) sees external forms?

Born and existing in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), being free from passion for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), without bringing the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) into manifestation, and without attending to the signs of appearance while still possessing the perception of that [formless state], he resolves upon external forms.
Those objects from which he is free from passion are external to him.
He is without the perception of internal form for two reasons:
because he has attained the formless attainments and perceives that attainment within himself, and because he does not attend to the sign of internal luminosity.
The remainder is as before. (H 73b2;
C 336c4) How does one dwell having personally realized and attained the beautiful liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*) with the body?
It is when, for example, a certain person here becomes a possessor of equanimity and mindfulness that are completely pure and cleansed.
And by relying upon that, the beautiful [perception] is cultivated until it becomes perfected in its noble form.
That is the beautiful liberation.
For what reason?
By three reasons:
because of the transcendence of pleasure and pain, because of the cessation of all agitation, and because of being well-cultivated.
"Having realized it with the body" means that by means of that dwelling, the noble ones dwell frequently.
The liberation of the sphere of infinite space is as follows: one who is free from passion for that [sphere] becomes resolved upon space itself.

Likewise, the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness belongs to one who is free from passion for that and becomes resolved upon it. For one who has attained the sphere of nothingness and becomes resolved upon the sphere of infinite consciousness, there is the liberation of the sphere of nothingness.
However, regarding the liberation of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), one does not resolve upon anything else.
As long as the perception of totality (*kṛtsnasaṃjñā*) arises, so long must one resolve [upon it].
Having first resolved and performed the preparatory cultivation (*parikarma*), one subsequently views [the object] having mastered it; thus they are called the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Furthermore, that overcoming (*abhibhava*) should be understood as fivefold.

Overcoming by means of inferiority is, for example, when someone, on account of some excellence such as a craft or the like, establishes another in a state of inferiority. Overcoming by weakening is, for example, when one who is stronger brings down one who is weaker.
Overpowering by means of concealment is, for example, when one renders something invisible by means of a vessel or the like, or conceals it through mantras or supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).

Overpowering by means of revulsion is, for example, when one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*) after having reviled them. Overpowering by means of mastery is, for example, when a master establishes a servant in a position according to his will for the purpose of acting as he desires.
In this context, however, what is intended is the mastery through concealment and the mastery through overpowering.
First, there is mastery over resolve regarding the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and subsequently, mastery over overpowering regarding the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Among these, "he sees forms that are limited" refers to those known as sentient beings and their requisites.
"Excessive" refers to houses, dwellings, and so forth.
"Beautiful" means those which are pleasing in color because they are exclusively pure;
by contrast, the opposite of these are "ugly."
Those which are inferior are unpleasant in terms of sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects. By the opposite of these, they are excellent.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of color among sentient beings, among their requisites, and among their celestial palaces.
"He knows having overcome" means that he resolves upon the object by repeatedly making it disappear. "And he possesses such a perception" means he possesses the perception of having overcome.
By means of the *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totality bases), one resolves upon the entire sphere (*āyatana*) as the basis for resolution.
In that regard, it is "non-dual" because for the noble one there is no distinction between self and what belongs to the self.
It is, however, "immeasurable" for all [beings].
For what reason is this established by means of the two bases of form and the tangible?
Because these two—[the attainment of cessation and the attainment of non-perception]—are possible everywhere within both one’s own and another’s continuum, and within all material realms;
whereas the eye and other [faculties] belong exclusively to one’s own continuum, and even odor and taste are not omnipresent.
Furthermore, for those material phenomena ending with the realm of form, the "total attainment" (*kṛtsnasamāpatti*) is the culmination of the realm of form.
Furthermore, in the formless realms, space is omnipresent;
therefore, the *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality sphere) is established therein,
because consciousness has the entirety of its object as its range.
First, the practitioner first forms a resolute conviction (*adhimucyate*); thereafter, he masters [the object].
Having attained mastery over that mastery, he subsequently forms a resolute conviction regarding that entire sense-sphere (*āyatana*) according to his wish.
Therefore, this is their sequential order.

H 74a2; C 337a18 (4.1.1.4.2) By means of the eight pure totalities of form (*rūpakṛtsna*), one brings forth noble supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) consisting of resolute intention (*ādhimokṣika*) and the transformation of objects (*vastupariṇāmika*).
Whatever he resolves upon, up to whatever he transforms, it becomes exactly so; and it is possible for him to perform a function with that [transformed object], such as gold and so forth.

By means of the completely purified totality of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṛtsna*), he brings forth the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), and so forth.
By means of the completely purified totality of space (*ākāśa-kṛtsna*), he makes space whatever he desires.
Just as, for example, potters, smiths, and goldsmiths first prepare clay and other materials, yet those [materials] have not yet been fully refined.
Thus is the stage of the liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Just as [objects] are well-prepared, so is the stage of the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Just as, having well-prepared them, they transform them at will, so should the stage of the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) be regarded.
(4.1.2.1.0) There are three concentrations: emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the wishless (*apraṇihita*), and the signless (*ānimitta*).
(4.1.2.1.1.1) What is the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*)?
It is the stability and one-pointedness of the mind with respect to the absence of a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, and a person.
(H 74a5; C 337a29, 4.1.2.1.1.2) In this regard, emptiness is fourfold:
emptiness as investigation, such as when one contemplates all phenomena as empty of permanence, up to and including a self or what belongs to a self.
Emptiness of that fruit is, for example, the emptiness of the unshakable liberation of mind from all afflictions such as passion.
Internal emptiness is, for example, the emptiness of the personal existence from the notions of "I," "mine," and the conceit "I am," as well as from dogmatic adherence.
External emptiness is, for example, the emptiness of the five strands of sensual pleasure from sensual passion.
As it has been said: "By completely transcending perceptions of form, having personally realized external emptiness with the body and attained it, I dwell therein," and so forth.
For here, "perceptions of form" refers to perceptions of the qualities of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
Because of the abandonment of the passion arising from those perceptions, that is called "external emptiness."

At times the yogin attends to external emptiness, at times to internal emptiness by means of the emptiness of its fruit, and at times to internal-external emptiness by means of the emptiness of examination; for it is by virtue of these that his mind enters into them.
If he does not even enter into internal-external emptiness (*adhyātmabahirdhāśūnyatā*), then he attends to the imperturbable (*āniñja*).
The perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*) or the perception of suffering (*duḥkhasaṃjñā*) is called "the imperturbable.
As he attends in this way, there is no movement of the thought "I am," and his mind does not waver in detail regarding "this is I" or "I am this."
Then his mind enters into those two.
(H 74b1; C 337b15) What is the wishless concentration of the mind (*apraṇihita-cetaḥsamādhi*)?
It is the stability and one-pointedness of the mind for one who attends to the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent or as suffering.
(4.1.2.1.3.1) What is the signless (*animitta*)?
It is the stability and one-pointedness of the mind of one who attends to the cessation of those very aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) as peaceful.
(4.1.2.1.3.2) As it was said in detail: "The signless concentration of mind is not depressed," and so forth.
In that regard, how is one neither bowed down nor bent forward?
Because of being dissociated from both opposition and compliance.
Furthermore, for two reasons, one enters the signless (*animitta*):

Because of the non-attention to all signs (*nimitta*) and the attention to the signless realm (*ānimittadhātu*), one does not feel revulsion toward nor disparage those signs when not attending to them; rather, one simply practices non-conditioning (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Therefore, it is called "not bending down" (*anavanata*).
And by attending to the signless realm, one does not become attached to it.
Therefore, one is said to be "not bent toward" it.
And that concentration is twofold: the preparatory and the fruit of preparation.
Among these, the preparatory is established through repeated careful discernment.
And he becomes unliberated from signs. For his consciousness, following after signs, remains from time to time seizing hold of the mind.
However, when that [consciousness] is repeatedly restrained through careful discernment, it takes up the fruit and is liberated from following after signs.
And because that which is liberated does not remain through analytical reflection due to its very nature of liberation, it is therefore "well-liberated" (*suvimukta*).
That which is repeatedly established through analytical reflection becomes liberated only because it remains [in that state], but it is not "well-liberated.

The "fruit of full knowledge" (*ājñāphala*) and the "benefit of full knowledge" (*ājñānuśaṃsa*) are so called because they bring about the abandonment of the afflictions and the dwelling in happiness in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Furthermore, cessation (*nirodha*) is also "higher knowledge" (*ājñā*), and the path (*mārga*) is also [higher knowledge];
from these two, respectively, there arise the fruit of higher knowledge (*ājñāphala*) and the benefit of higher knowledge (*ājñānuśaṃsa*).
Moreover, the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) is also higher knowledge, and arhatship (*arhattva*) is also higher knowledge.
In that regard, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is the fruit of full knowledge (*ājñāphala*), while the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*) is the benefit of full knowledge (*ājñānuśaṃsa*).
Because one perceives that whatever is not present in a certain place is empty of that, there is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
One who sees in this way does not form a directed aspiration toward that very [object], and thus it is the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
One sees that which is free from the signs (*nimitta*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); thus, it is "signless" (*ānimitta*).
Why, then, is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) mentioned first here, whereas elsewhere it is said that "what is impermanent is suffering, and what is suffering is non-self," with emptiness coming later?

It is because the vision of impermanence and suffering is not purified in such a way as to result in the absence of longing (*apraṇidhāna*) until the perception of non-self (*anātmasaṃjñā*) is firmly established.
Immediately after that, there is non-aspiration.
For this very reason it is said in detail: "For one who possesses the perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self becomes established.
Having seen that as impermanent and non-self, he does not aspire toward it.
"Seeking the escape, he directs his attention precisely toward the signless (*animitta*)," thus the signless is mentioned immediately thereafter.
H 74b7; C 337c17 (4.1.2.2.1) What is concentration with applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*)?
It is that which is associated with applied and sustained thought.
(4.1.2.2.2) What is concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only (*avitarko vicāramātraḥ samādhi*)?
It is that which is associated with sustained thought only; by cultivating this, one attains the state of Mahābrahmā.
(4.1.2.2.3) What is concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarko ’vicāraḥ samādhi*)?

That which is dissociated from applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), by cultivating which one is reborn above that point, up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), except for the untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative absorptions.
How does concentration become without applied thought and without sustained thought?

Having looked with equanimity upon the mind regarding applied and sustained thought, if one resolves upon an internal object with a single flavor and it becomes manifest with a single flavor, [then it is so].

(4.1.2.3.1.1) What is limited concentration (*parīttaḥ samādhiḥ*)? It is limited either by way of its object (*ālambana*), because it perceives forms that are limited in scope, or by way of mental attention (*manasikāra*), because it possesses limited faith, aspiration, and resolve. (4.1.2.3.1.2) What is exalted concentration (*mahadgataḥ samādhiḥ*)?
It is "vast" either by way of its object (*ālambana*), because of the perception of abundant forms, but not because of the perception of the infinite;

or it is "vast" by way of mental attention (*manasikāra*), because of the presence of excessive faith, desire, and resolve (*adhimokṣa*), but not because of faith, desire, and resolve that are infinite and boundless.
What is the immeasurable concentration (*apramāṇa-samādhi*)?

Either by way of the object (*ālambana*), because of seeing forms that are infinite and boundless; or by way of mental attention (*manasikāra*), because of having faith, desire, and resolve (*adhimokṣa*) that are infinite and boundless.
In this regard, the "exalted" concentration of mind (*mahadgata-cetaḥsamādhi*) is as follows: one resolves upon a single tree-root, thinking, "The Ābhā devas, the Ābhā devas," and so forth in detail.
The immeasurables are the four immeasurables.
Regarding the phrase "the Ābhā gods, the Ābhā gods," how does one resolve upon a single tree root?
Having become disgusted with the desire realm, one who has attained the first *dhyāna* applies himself to purifying that meditative attainment.
He has also heard that there are the Ābhā gods.

As he attends to the appearance of their physical forms, he resolves upon the root of a single tree, and so on, until the entire earth bounded by the ocean, due to the progressive intensification of his meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
A distinction in rebirth arises from the specific excellence of that [concentration].
H 75a5; C 338a11 (4.1.2.3.3.2) How does the twofold nature of attention arise?
To whatever extent one has conviction, to that same extent attention is designated for that person.
How, depending on the twofold nature of attention, does the twofold nature of cultivation arise?

By the power of that very mental attention (*manasikāra*), a distinction in the cultivation of that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is designated, due to its becoming increasingly and most purely refined. How is it that, based on the two degrees of cultivation, the two types of practice (*pratipad*) are designated?
To the extent that the meditative concentration becomes more thoroughly cultivated, to that same extent a distinction in the cause for rebirth (*upapatti-hetu*) is designated.
How is it that, based on the mere existence of two paths, the mere existence of two types of persons is designated?
For that reason, among the beings born there, the distinctions of high and low, or inferior and superior, are designated.
What is the difference in radiance between the first and second dhyānas?

Just as the radiance of a gem exists outside the gem, while the gem itself is not the radiance, so too in the first dhyāna there is radiance outside the body, but the bodies themselves are not the radiance.
However, just as the radiance of a lamp exists outside the lamp and that lamp is the light, so too in the second dhyāna the body itself should be understood as the radiance.
For this very reason, they are said to be "of one-body" (*ekatvakāya*) therein.
H 75b1; C 338a25 (4.1.2.3.4.1) How is the establishment of the four immeasurables (apramāṇa) effected?
There are three kinds of sentient beings:
those who are neither suffering nor happy, those who are suffering, and those who are happy.
They, in their respective order, are those who desire happiness, those who desire separation from suffering, and those who desire non-separation from happiness.

For them, four [aspects] are established through a fourfold application: respectively, through the application of happiness, the application of removing suffering, and the application of rejoicing in the non-separation from happiness for the [first] three.

Equanimity (*upekṣā*), moreover, consists in the withdrawal from the three aforementioned desires for pleasure and so forth by means of the absence of affliction through dissatisfaction and longing, the absence of affliction through hatred, and the absence of affliction through attachment—

[expressed] as "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness" (*maitrīsahagatena cittena*), and so forth. In that context, it is "accompanied by loving-kindness" because it is present as a state of rendering assistance.
For a friend is characterized by helpfulness.
And helpfulness is twofold: the provision of welfare and the provision of happiness.
And those two are illuminated by all the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
"Without enmity" means because of the absence of malice in one's disposition (*āśaya*). "Without rivalry" means because of abiding in a state free from opposition.
"By non-affliction" means by not engaging in harmful actions.
"Vast" means because of the greatness of its objective support (*ālambana*).
"Exalted" means because of the predominance of bringing about welfare and happiness.
"Immeasurable" means that there is no limit to its fruition, like the confluence of the waters of the four great rivers.
"Well-cultivated" means because it has been thoroughly mastered.
Furthermore, as to what kind of mind it is—such as that accompanied by loving-kindness—he says:
"Having resolved upon and pervaded [it], having attained" means having suffused it with the resolve of superior intention (*adhyāśaya-adhimokṣa*).
"Having attained" means having purified and cleansed it.
"Dwells" means by way of passing the time through the practice of spending the nights and days.
Regarding what was stated—that loving-kindness (*maitrī*), when cultivated, becomes supremely pure—and so forth: with what intention was this said?
This is the pinnacle of all pleasures, namely the third *dhyāna*.
Loving-kindness, when thoroughly cultivated through the attainment of that [state], becomes supreme.
Therefore, it is called "supreme purity.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) also becomes supreme when cultivated through the application of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). For its intention is the application of removing suffering.

Therefore, because all this—such as the suffering of cutting and piercing—is entirely absent in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), one who has entered into compassion directs sentient beings who are suffering toward the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), thinking:
"May they be in that place where suffering, together with its basis, does not exist.
Furthermore, one who has entered into sympathetic joy (*muditā*) directs those sentient beings who are happy and have attained joy toward the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
"May there be such immeasurable happiness for these beings, up to the immeasurable sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
In this way, sympathetic joy (*muditā*), when cultivated through the application of the sphere of infinite consciousness, becomes supreme.
And this is the limit of the stage of untainted mind (*anāsravacittabhūmi*), namely, the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
And that is the supreme among forms of equanimity.

Therefore, having entered into equanimity with the thought, "Just as for an Arhat monk there is non-affliction in all movements of pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure, so may it be for these sentient beings," his equanimity— cultivated by the application of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)— becomes supreme.
H 75b7; C 338c2 (4.1.2.3.4.3.5) Furthermore, all these noble aspects, accompanied by the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), can be cultivated only by a noble one (*ārya*).
H 75b7; C 338c5 (4.1.2.4.1.1) What is concentration cultivated in a single part (*ekāṃśabhāvita*)?
It is that wherein one enters meditative attainment having attended to either a sign of illumination (*avabhāsanimitta*) or a sign of form (*rūpanimitta*).
By means of those two, one either perceives the radiance or sees forms, respectively.
What is the meditative concentration cultivated in both aspects? It is that which one enters by attending to both.
He perceives light and sees forms.
H 76a1; C 338c9 (4.1.2.4.2.1) Thus, for one whose concentration is cultivated by means of light, eleven obstacles—doubt and the rest—are to be understood in detail exactly as in the Sūtra.
But of what are these the obstacles?
Regarding the two kinds of signs for concentration—namely, the sign of the object (*ālambana-nimitta*) and the sign of the cause (*nidāna-nimitta*)—concentration remains by depending upon them.
For one who has fallen away from that sign, it does not remain.
In this regard, first, because of the manifestation of the appearance of form which was previously unperceived, there arises doubt.
(4.1.2.4.2.2.2) Non-attention arises from a state of laxity;
just as one who does not wish to see forms either closes their eyes or turns their face away, so too does this person fall into non-attention toward those forms.
(4.1.2.4.2.2.3) Physical corruption arises from such things as failing to guard the doors of the sense faculties.
From excessive wakefulness or from indulging in excessive sleep, there arises dullness, namely, lethargy and torpor.
For one who does not see forms or sees them incompletely, one exerts excessive application for the sake of both [seeing clearly], and performs an excessively constrained mental attention;
therefore, there is overly exerted vigor.
(4.1.2.4.2.2.6) Furthermore, due to the fault of excessive exertion (*atyārambha*), he makes [the mind] overly slack, like the crushing of a *laṭukikā* bird.

(4.1.2.4.2.2.7) For one who seeks merely its appearance, that [appearance] arises simultaneously with the seeing of forms; thus, by desiring one thing, there is the attainment of two, like finding two openings to a treasure.
(4.1.2.4.2.2.8) Because gentle forms suddenly appear in all directions, there is simultaneous paralysis (*śambitatva*), like the simultaneous flight of owls situated on both sides.
As he walks or dwells among the wonders of the world, a perception of diversity arises in him.
That external perception creates an obstacle for his concentration.
Or again, by means of that concentration, seeing himself as superior and others as inferior, he exalts himself.
This too is the perception of diversity.

(4.1.2.4.2.2.10) When one who has applied oneself excessively to speech or who reflects for too long becomes physically exhausted before the mind reaches concentration, this is excessive verbalization (*atyabhijalpa*).

(4.1.2.4.2.2.11) When there arises the appearance of a sign in the perception of forms, one abandons the mental attention directed toward the internal dwelling in yoga and directs it outwardly toward forms.
"He began to reflect closely" (*upanidhyātum ārabhata*)—this state of excessive reflection is an obstacle to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

These [factors] should be understood, as appropriate, as obstacles to the object (*ālambana*) of concentration and as obstacles to its cause (*nidāna*), because one is displaced from the object and the cause by means of their respective signs (*nimitta*), in due order.
Some cause one to fall away from both signs.

(4.1.2.5.1) What is concentration accompanied by joy (*prītisahagata-samādhi*)? It is the concentration present in the first and second meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). (4.1.2.5.2) What is concentration accompanied by pleasure (*sātasahagata-samādhi*)?
In the third dhyāna. What is concentration accompanied by equanimity?
It begins from the fourth dhyāna onwards.
(4.1.2.6.1) What is the cultivation of concentration that leads to dwelling in happiness in the present life?

It is the cultivation of concentration on the path of preparation for the four dwellings in happiness in the present life, as well as the cultivation of concentration during the fundamental states when they are not yet purified or cleansed.
However, the Blessed One has taught the path of preparation for the first dhyāna specifically for the purpose of attaining a previously unattained meditative attainment.
H 76b1; C 339a14 (4.1.2.6.2) What is the cultivation of concentration that leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision?
Here, a monk has properly and thoroughly grasped the sign of light, as described in the Sūtra.
This should be understood as the path of application for the realization of the divine eye.
In this context, that which is the observation of forms and their manifestation through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is "vision" (*darśana*).
Furthermore, that which is the knowledge—detailed in the *Adhidevatāsūtra*—that "those deities have such names, such a birth," and so forth, is "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
(H 76b2; C 339a19) What kind of cultivation of concentration (*samādhibhāvanā*) conduces to the differentiation of wisdom (*prajñā*)?
The cultivation of concentration on the path of preparation for the realization of truth and for the fruit of stream-entry, as well as that of the analytical knowledges.
(H 76b2; C 339a21, 4.1.2.6.4) What is the cultivation of concentration that leads to the destruction of the outflows?
It is that which occurs on the path of preparation for the fruit of arhatship.
(4.1.2.7.0) What is the noble meditative concentration consisting of fivefold knowledge?
This meditative concentration of mine is indeed noble, free from worldly gain, and free from material substratum—this is explained in detail according to the Sūtra.

By this, fivefold knowledge is elucidated, namely: knowledge by way of intrinsic nature, by way of the person, by way of purification, by way of the fruit, and knowledge regarding the signs for emerging from meditative concentration.
(4.1.2.7.1) In this context, "noble" (*ārya*) refers both to noble virtue (*kuśalāryatā*) and to noble freedom from outflows (*anāsravāryatā*).
"Free from worldly gain" (*nirāmiṣa*) makes known the noble virtue, while "free from substrate" (*niraupadhika*) makes known the noble freedom from outflows.
(4.1.2.7.2) "Not practiced by base persons" (*akāpuruṣasevita*) means [practiced] by the noble ones—the Buddhas and their disciples.
"Commended by the wise" means by those very [wise ones].
"Not censured by the wise" is because it is praised at all times.
It is not like the first dhyāna, which is first praised as peaceful for the sake of striving toward higher progress, but later censured as coarse.
It is "peaceful" because the afflictions that are its opposites have been stilled.
It is "excellent" because there is no relishing of the afflictions belonging to its own level.
It is "one who has attained the path of relaxation" because of the attainment of a path from which there is no falling away.
"Attained through the one-pointedness of mind" means because of the attainment of the stage free from applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra*).
"Pleasurable in the present" means because it is an abiding in happiness in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
"Having a ripening of happiness in the future" means because it brings about the bliss of *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*).

(4.1.2.7.5) “I shall attain [absorption] while mindful” is due to the non-forgetting of the well-grasped sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*). “I shall emerge while mindful” is due to the non-forgetting of the well-grasped sign of emergence (*vyutthānanimitta*). (4.1.2.8.0) What is the five-limbed concentration (*pañcāṅgika-samādhi*)?
(4.1.2.8.1.1) Here, a monk [perceives] this very body with the joy and happiness born of seclusion—that is, belonging to the level of the first dhyāna.

Therein, he drenches it with joy and saturates it with happiness. He suffuses it during the mental application that reaches the culmination of practice, and he thoroughly gladdens it during the preceding mental applications.
For even in those [lower stages], joy and bliss arise from time to time, yet they are neither stable nor complete.
In the mental application that is the fruit of the culmination of practice (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala-manaskāra*), there is nothing whatsoever that remains unclear or that requires further pervasion.
In this context, just as there is a skilled bath-attendant or his apprentice, so should the practitioner of yoga (yogācāra) be regarded.
The instruction and admonition should be understood as beginning with the joy and bliss born of seclusion from sensual desires, [likened to] a bronze vessel, a metal basin, or a shell.
The fine bath-powders should be understood as the thoughts of renunciation and so forth that are conducive to that state.
Having sprinkled the chariot, the path of the purification of discursive thought is to be seen.
The "bathing mound" is to be seen as the body;
it is moist due to its connection with joy, and it is permeated by moisture due to its connection with pleasure.
"Manifest both internally and externally" indicates a state of union with uninterrupted joy and bliss;
"not spreading outward" means due to the absence of distraction;
and "not overflowing" means due to the absence of affliction and the absence of relishing [the experience].
In the second [case], a specific qualification of the simile is to be observed. Therein, the concentration accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*) is like the mountain;
above that is the second dhyāna, which is without applied thought (*avitarka*), because of the resolution (*adhimokṣa*) upon the single flavor of the object through its condensation.
By means of internal serenity, it is like a lake:
that outflow of water on the side which has water as its source is the "water-eye";
that upward-flowing outflow of water is the "water-ford."
By means of these two, he demonstrates joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) respectively.
Terms such as "overflowing" (*abhiṣyandana*) and so forth are as explained previously.
There is no lack of clarity because of its uninterrupted application.
In the third case as well, there is a specific distinction regarding the illustration.
In that context, just as with the blue lotus and so forth, so too is the pleasure devoid of rapture (*niṣprītika*), the mental factors associated with it, and its physical basis (*āśraya*).
The concentration (*samādhi*) devoid of rapture and lacking both applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra*) is comparable to the water.
Joy is that which produces exhilaration;
because of its absence, [the seeds] are said to have their husks submerged.
In the fourth [case] as well, there is a specific distinction regarding the simile.
In that context, "with a purified mind" means being associated with the purification of equanimity and mindfulness through the transcendence of the defects of the lower stages.
"With a cleansed [mind]" means being wholesome (*kuśala*) due to the absence of relishing the defilements of its own stage.
Furthermore, for what purpose is the simile of the householder given?
For he is skillful, of a heedful nature, a thinker, a weigher, and an investigator; and nothing remains unknown to him, whether it be income or expenditure.

In the same way, one who has attained the pure fourth dhyāna becomes skillful, intent on heedfulness, and adept in discerning all matters. By the phrase "woven eightfold or ninefold," he shows that because of its density, it is impenetrable to gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like.
The phrase "together with head and feet" would be understood through two possible defects:
either because of the thinness of the garment or because of the exposure of the naked parts;
he demonstrates the absence of both of these.

In the same way, being suffused by that completely purified mind, he becomes inaccessible to all disturbances; he is patient toward cold and heat, up to shouts of "ha" and "phi," harsh words from others, and even physical sensations.
This is the fifth specific illustration.
It should be understood that the phrase "the sign of contemplation itself, well and thoroughly" is exactly as explained previously.
He contemplates the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the three time periods, and he also contemplates that by which he contemplates—this is the summary meaning therein.
What is this noble concentration (*ārya-samādhi*)?
How is the fivefold arrangement established?
(H 77b2; C 339c24) That one-pointedness of mind of the noble ones in the four dhyānas and during the state of analytical observation is the noble concentration.
(H 77b2; C 339c26) The establishment of these as factors is based on their role in the four abidings in happiness in the present life.
Because it pertains to the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the fifth factor is established for the sake of abandoning the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Thus, its establishment should be understood by way of two reasons. (H 77b3;
C 339c29) What is noble right concentration (*āryasamyaksamādhi*) together with its proximate cause and its equipment?
In this context, one is called "noble" (ārya) because of being noble through wholesome and untainted [states].
For such a person, there are five factors of the path as its proximate cause:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
And there are three requisites: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
These, taken together, were spoken of by the Blessed One:
The seven factors of the path are said to be both the proximate cause (*upaniṣad*) and the equipment (*pariṣkāra*) for noble right concentration;
however, they should be understood according to their respective applications.
In that regard, five are the proximate cause in the sense of being the preliminary sequence, while three are the equipment in the sense of being the requisites for concentration.
H 77b4; C 340a7 (4.1.2.9.3) How does right view become the precursor?
Having known that there are in the world Arhats who have attained the goal correctly, one generates the desire for renunciation.
Having acquired right view, one then forms the intention for renunciation.
"The household life is a confinement," and so on in detail.
Having gone forth from there, he purifies his ethical discipline and his livelihood;
these become for him right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Furthermore, for such a person, the five adversaries of right view and the other [factors]—namely, wrong view and so forth—are as yet unabandoned.

Relying upon and established in these very same five wholesome factors, he generates the right view consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī samyagdṛṣṭi*) through the influence of another's voice, which serves as the equipment for the path (*mārgasaṃbhāra*) for the sake of abandoning those adversarial factors.
Relying upon that hearing-based [view], he then generates the [right view] consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*).
Relying upon that which consists of reflection, one generates that which consists of cultivation.

By means of that right view, one understands wrong view as it truly is from the perspective of wrong view, and right view as it truly is from the perspective of right view; having fully understood everything up to right livelihood, one generates enthusiasm for the abandonment of wrong view and so forth, and for the attainment of right view and so forth.
That by which he brings about the abandonment of those opposing factors and the full attainment (*upasampad*) of those qualities is his right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
And that mindfulness, being a constituent part of concentration (*samādhi-bhāga*), is said to be "concentration" in the sense previously described.

In that interval during which one abandons wrong view and the like, and fully attains right view and the like, one also abandons wrong effort and wrong mindfulness on the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) and [attains] right effort and right mindfulness. Simultaneously with the abandonment and attainment of those, the noble right concentration becomes perfected.
In that regard, wisdom, acting as a precursor, applies itself to higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).

That which is the mental attention based on reasoning following the voice of another, and that which is the training in higher ethics—relying upon both of these, the training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom arise on the path of preparation.
Therein, right mindfulness is the training in higher mind;
right view and right effort are the training in higher wisdom.
The fulfillment of these three trainings occurs at the time of noble right concentration.
What is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*)?
It is the final concentration of all those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
Because it is foremost, supreme, essential, unconquerable by secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and unconquerable by the primary afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called "diamond-like" (*vajropama*).
Just as a diamond is the essence of all gems and is not scratched by anything, yet scratches everything—this is its similarity to a diamond.
What are the five attainments of vision (*darśanasamāpatti*)?
"In this case, a monk [contemplates] this very body," and so on in detail as in the Sūtra.
These are called "the attainments of vision" (*darśanasamāpatti*) because they belong to one who has attained vision.

Their complete body should be understood as consisting of: the counteragent that suppresses what is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), the counteragent that abandons (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*), and the analytical inspection of abandonment (*prahāṇapratyavekṣā*).

(4.1.3.1.2) Therein, by means of the first [application], relying on the application of mindfulness consisting in the practice of the foul (*aśubha-prāyogika-smṛtyupasthāna*), one contemplates the foulness of the internal body so that sensual desire does not arise.

By means of the second [application], relying on that very same [practice] up to the contemplation of the skeleton-man (*asthipuruṣa*), one contemplates the foulness of the external body so that that very [sensual desire] does not arise.
To this extent, the foulness of all [bodies] has been contemplated.
In this context, "piercing through, piercing through" means having transcended the sequence of methods for examining the livid corpse and so forth.
By means of the former [contemplation], one reflects upon the impurity currently present within the body; by means of the latter, one penetrates the true nature (*dharmatā*):
"This body, too, is of such a nature and shares such a lot," and so on in detail.
(4.1.3.1.3) "He contemplates the stream of consciousness" means that he contemplates its arising and passing away.

He contemplates consciousness conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) from the perspective of the linking of successive births, and from the perspective of the linking of successive moments, in such ways as "possessing passion" or "free from passion.
Having passed through various nights and days, and various moments, instants, and hours, he contemplates how "one thing indeed arises and another ceases," in many kinds and numerous diverse ways.

(4.1.3.1.4) In this regard, a learner (*śaikṣa*) who is not yet free from passion contemplates that which is established in both worlds; one who is free from passion contemplates it only from the perspective of the next world; and an Arhat contemplates it as being established nowhere at all.
This is their contemplation regarding abandonment.
(4.1.3.2) The attainments of the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) have been explained previously.

(4.1.3.3.1) The attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñāsamāpatti*) is the cessation of the mind and mental factors through a mental orientation preceded by the perception of liberation, [achieved] by one who is free from passion for the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven] but not yet free from passion for what is above it. (4.1.3.3.2) Furthermore, how does one enter that attainment?

Thinking, “Perception is a disease, perception is an abscess, perception is a thorn,” one who has attained the fourth dhyāna cultivates a mental attention that turns away from perception; he remains turned away from every perception as soon as it arises.
Thinking, “This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the state of non-perception (asaṃjñika),” he directs his mind toward the state of non-perception.
In this way, through gradual withdrawal from all objects of focus, the mind is brought to cessation.
In this case, one who has been reborn there both enters into and emerges from [the meditative attainment].
There, having been reborn, one remains in a state of having already entered [the attainment]; and through the arising of perception, there occurs a falling away from that state for them.
(4.1.3.4.1) What is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?

It is the cessation of the mind and mental factors through a mental attention preceded by the perception of dwelling, in one who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
(4.1.3.4.2) Furthermore, how does one enter that [attainment]?

An noble one who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness may have entered the signless attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or the signless attainment of cessation.

In that regard, for one who has entered the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and is looking with equanimity upon what lies beyond it, the mind—having moved away from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—is a mind whose objective support has been completely ceased; the same applies to one who has entered the signless attainment of cessation.
For one entering the attainment of cessation, two factors are of great assistance:
serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). In that regard, what is serenity?

What is insight (vipaśyanā)? How do these two become so very beneficial? In this context, tranquility (śamatha) refers to the eight successive attainments, and insight refers to noble wisdom (prajñā).
Due to the deficiency of either one of these, there is no attainment (*samāpatti*). Both, having come together, are of great utility.
(H 78b4; C 340c22) For one entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), how do the three formations (*saṃskāra*) cease in successive order?
This is twofold: movement and dwelling.
Therein, while engaged in movement, one may even engage in conversation.
In that regard, the activity of the first dhyāna exists because of the presence of vocal formations (*vāk-saṃskāra*).
However, when one begins the meditative dwelling, then, starting from the second dhyāna, there is a successive cessation through successive attainments.
Likewise, in the process of emergence, the arising should be understood as occurring in reverse order.
(4.1.3.4.3.3) For one who has entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the mind and mental factors have ceased.
How is it that consciousness has not departed from the body?

Because, while his material sense faculties remain untransformed, the *ālayavijñāna*—which is sustained by the seeds of the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*)—continues without interruption, so that they may arise again in the future.
How is it that for one entering the attainment of cessation, there does not occur the thought:
“I am entering cessation” or “I am emerging”?
Because at the time of entry, the mind ceases without volitional effort (*nirabhisaṃskāra*), and because at the time of emergence, the mind has already ceased previously.
How has that mind been previously prepared by him?

Because he has cultivated and frequently practiced those aspects, signs, and marks through which the attainment and emergence [from meditative absorption] occur, he enters and emerges from it spontaneously due to their having been developed.
(4.1.3.4.3.5) How does one who has emerged from cessation experience three types of contact?
Is it immovable, nothingness, and signless?
For the most part, when emerging from that attainment, one emerges by means of three kinds of objects:
the object of existence, the object of sensory domains, and the object of cessation.
And as he emerges from those [attainments], he experiences three types of contact in their proper order.
Among these, for one emerging by taking existence (*bhava*) as the object, there is no wavering of the mind—namely, the detailed elaboration: "I am," or "this is who I am," or "I shall be."
Therefore, it is said that he touches the touch of the immovable (*ānijya*).
For one who emerges from meditative absorption by taking an object as a focal point, there is no trace of passion (*rāga*), no trace of hatred (*dveṣa*), and no trace of delusion (*moha*).
Therefore, it is said that he touches the touch of nothingness (*ākiṃcanya*).

Emerging from [meditative absorption] by taking cessation as its object, one takes the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*) as an object because of the non-attention (*amanasikāra*) toward all signs (*nimitta*).
Therefore, it is said that "one touches the signless contact (*animitta-sparśa*).
The meditations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*) have been explained.

H 79a2; C 341a24 (4.2.1) Regarding what was said by the Blessed One: “Bhikṣus, apply yourselves to yoga for the sake of seclusion, for the sake of inner tranquility of mind,” therein, when one dwells in secluded lodgings—whether having gone to the forest or so forth—and sits down, having established mindfulness directed toward the goal in detail, this is seclusion (*pratisaṃlayana*); and this is the physical withdrawal (*kāyavyavakarṣa*).
The ninefold abiding of the mind within is internal mental serenity (*adhyātma-cetaḥ-śamatha*);
this is the withdrawal of the mind. In that regard, seclusion brings about internal mental serenity, and internal mental serenity, in turn, brings about insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Vipaśyanā brings about the clear manifestation of phenomena as they truly are for one who has mastered [the practice].

Regarding what was said by the Blessed One: “Monks, cultivate concentration—immeasurable, steadfast, and mindful”—having thus stated the general heading “cultivate concentration,” he demonstrates its threefold cultivation.
In that context, "immeasurable" refers to the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
"The steadfast" (*nipaka*) refers to what is called steadfastness (*naipakya*), which consists of constant practice and skillful practice.
"The mindful" (*pratismṛta*) illuminates the state of having a mind established in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
H 79a4; C 341b12 (4.2.2.2) Why is there a threefold instruction on cultivation?
There are these two perfections: the mundane and the supramundane.
In this regard, the cultivation of the immeasurables brings about the worldly [attainment], mindfulness brings about the supramundane, and skillfulness brings about swift direct knowledge for both;
for this very reason, it is taught between these two; and only this triad is to be taught.

Furthermore, "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) illuminates the path of calm abiding (*śamatha*); "mindful" (*pratismṛta*) illuminates the path of insight (*vipaśyanā*); and "vigilant" (*nipaka*) illuminates the path of their swift realization.
Moreover, it illuminates the practice leading to merit, the practice leading to nirvāṇa, and the practice leading to the swift attainment of those two.
For one who has previously mastered calm abiding and subsequently cultivates concentration accompanied by insight, the objects of knowledge are correctly discerned as they truly are.
(4.2.3.0) As it was said by the Blessed One:
“There is a meditator who is skilled in concentration (*samādhi*) but not skilled in meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),” and so forth, as detailed in the summary verse of the sutra.
(4.2.3.1.1) How does one become skilled in concentration?
Because of proficiency in the three meditative concentrations beginning with emptiness (*śūnyatā*),
how could one not be skilled in meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)?
[One would be so] if one were not skilled in the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
How is one skilled in meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) but not skilled in concentrations (*samādhi*)?
One is skilled in entering into and emerging from the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), as well as the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñāsamāpatti*), but not in the three concentrations.
Because of being skilled in both, one is skilled in both; because of not being skilled in both, one is not skilled in both.
Thus, these aforementioned meditative concentrations and attainments should be applied in such a way that whichever one a person is suited for, they apply themselves accordingly.
Furthermore, it says:
"One becomes skilled in meditative concentration."
One knows the meditative absorption by way of its names, phrases, and syllables, but not those aspects, marks, and signs of that attainment by which the attainment occurs.
How is one skilled in attainment but not skilled in concentration?

It is when someone here knows the aspects, marks, and signs of a particular concentration by which one enters it, yet having so entered, does not know that concentration by way of its names, phrases, and syllables.
"I have entered into this and that concentration"—

there are hundreds and thousands of such concentrations that a bodhisattva enters, yet he does not know their names, phrases, or syllables, thinking, "I have entered into this and that concentration," until he hears them from a Buddha or from bodhisattvas who have attained the supreme perfections, or until he himself has attained those perfections.
H 79b3; C 341c15 (4.2.3.2) What is stability (*sthiti*)?
It is when those aspects (*ākāra*), signs (*liṅga*), and marks (*nimitta*) by which one enters meditative attainment are well-grasped.
Because they are well-grasped, for as long as one desires, one remains in attainment and does not fall away from that concentration.
Thus, the dwelling of one who has attained [meditative absorption] and the non-falling away from it constitute this twofold stability.
(H 79b4; C 341c18, 4.2.3.3.1) What is emergence (*vyutthāna*)?

It is when, for instance, a certain person here, having disregarded those aspects, signs, and marks by which he entered [absorption], attends to a phenomenon belonging to the non-concentrated level—one not comprised within the body of conceptualization, and dissimilar to the concentrated level.

He emerges from that concentration for the sake of what must be done, or for the sake of what is necessary to be done, or for the sake of what has been undertaken as something to be done. In this context, "what must be done" refers, for example, to the work concerning robes, the alms-bowl, and personal requisites.
In this context, "what is necessary to be done" refers to the activities such as voiding excrement and urine, going for alms, and attending upon one's teachers.
In that regard, what is to be done by way of formal undertaking is as follows: suppose someone has made a certain proposition;
he then engages in some activity toward another by virtue of that undertaking.
Or again, if he desires to enter another meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), he emerges from the present one.

(4.2.3.4.1) In that regard, what are the aspects (*ākāra*)? They are the aspects—such as coarseness, calmness, disease, abscess, thorn, impermanence, and so forth—which one enters into while attending to the object of focus within this or that meditative concentration (*samādhi*). (4.2.3.4.2) What are the signs (*liṅga*)?

When he is close to attaining meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), then signs of that absorption arise for him, by which he knows: "Before long, I shall either enter or have entered such and such an absorption. His teacher as well, by those same signs, knows this.
"Before long, he will enter into such and such a meditative attainment.
What are the signs?
There are two signs: [text continues].
The sign of the object (*ālambananimitta*) and the sign of the cause (*nidānanimitta*).
(H 79b7; C 342a5) Therein, the sign of the object is the body of conceptualization (*vikalpaśarīra*), by means of which object one enters meditative attainment.

(H 80a1; C 342a6) The sign of the cause is that equipment for concentration (*samādhisambhāra*) by means of which one enters attainment, namely: concordant instruction, the accumulation of the equipment for concentration, and that which is accompanied by cultivation.

Zeal, a state of mental agitation, focused attention on the thorough knowledge of distraction and non-distraction, and freedom from interference by others—whether human or non-human, whether caused by sound or by activity.
H 80a1; C 342a11 (4.2.3.5.1) What is fitness (*kalyatā*)?

It is when one’s concentration is held together by volitional effort (*saṃskāra*) like water being supported [in a vessel], rather than being held by the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); it is neither peaceful, nor sublime, nor has the path been attained through tranquility, nor is there [calm] of the mind.
Having attained one-pointedness, his concentration is not fit for dwelling in ease. By the opposite, it becomes fit.
(H 80a2; C 342a15) How is he one who is constrained by conditioned formations (*saṃskārābhinigṛhīta*)?
With a volition accompanied by aspiration, he restrains the mind from the external and settles it within that concentration;
and for him who has become thus, that mental attention proceeds with effortful application (*sābhoga-vāhana*), so that it does not allow the mind to flow outward, being held like water in a vessel.
How does one become constrained by the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)?
One has perceived the coarse nature of phenomena below and the peaceful nature of phenomena above.
This is the attainment of the one-pointedness of mind, having realized the path that is peaceful, sublime, and tranquilized—just like the noble fivefold wisdom-concentration (*pañcajñānika-samādhi*).
H 80a3; C 342a21 (4.2.3.6) What is the range (*gocara*)?

It is the object (*viṣaya*) of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Because one who has attained [a state] beyond that does not know it—for example, one who has attained the first dhyāna does not see the second dhyāna—in the same way, one does not know that which transcends the faculties (*indriya*) and the person (*pudgala*).
(4.2.3.7) What is accomplishment (*abhinirhāra*)?

It is the condensation of the meaning of extensive words and phrases, as well as the production of distinguished qualities. (4.2.3.8.1) What is the excellence of meditative concentration (*samādhisāṃpreya*)?

Namely: moral shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), affection and reverence, faith, appropriate mental attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), mindfulness and clear comprehension (*smṛti-saṃprajanya*), restraint of the sense faculties, restraint of ethical conduct, and so forth, up to the culmination in happiness;
for the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. By the opposite [of these], it should be understood as that which is not conducive to welfare (*asāmpreyam*).

(4.2.3.8.3) Concordance and discordance: For instance, one may be endowed with some of these qualities such as shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), while not being endowed with others; that is, one possesses shame and dread of blame, yet is not joined with affection (*prema*) and reverence (*gaurava*). This is the detailed explanation. (4.2.3.9.1) What is acquisition (*āya*)?
The increase of the concentration already attained. What is decline? It is the loss of concentration.
What is skillful means (*upāya*)?
It is the path that leads to both of those.
Calm abiding (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are to be understood exactly as they were explained in the context of the signs for calm abiding and so forth.
H 80a6; C 342b5 (4.2.4.0) There is a meditator who perceives misfortune even when there is success; this is explained at length in the *Catuṣparivarta-dhyāyivibhaṅga-sūtra*.
In that regard, error is to be fully understood in two periods:
when concentration is declining and when it is progressing toward excellence.

In this context, the path leading to decline and decline itself constitute misfortune (*vipatti*); the path leading to distinction and the progression toward distinction constitute prosperity (*saṃpatti*).
How does it occur for him?
"Is the joy and bliss born of seclusion diminishing for me? Is my concentration falling away?
Here, through the sequence of cultivation, the mind of the meditator inclines toward tranquility;
thus, by being followed by equanimity, he enters the threshold of the second dhyāna from the first dhyāna.
And that [state] of his becomes unwholesome.
In that state, he has transcended the joy and bliss belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, yet he has not yet attained that which belongs to the level of the second dhyāna.
It occurs to him thus:
"The joy and bliss born of seclusion are diminishing for me.
He withdraws his mind from that [object].
That meditator must thoroughly understand that perversion therein.
H 80b1; C 342b16 (4.2.4.1.2) How is error to be fully understood when meditative concentration is declining?
In this case, a certain person becomes an attainer of the first dhyāna attainment, having accumulated the necessary provisions starting from [the perspective of] nirvāṇa.

Having reached that state of complete provision for nirvāṇa, by that cause and by that condition, through its impetus and by his own natural inclination, there arise in him such perceptions and mental attentions as these:

By means of those perceptions and mental attentions, whatever there is therein belonging to the category of form, up to and including that belonging to the category of consciousness, that appears to him as a disease, and so on, up to appearing as non-self.
And by relying upon that perception and mental attention, the joy and bliss born of worldly meditative attainment (*laukikasamāpatti*) no longer manifest for him; yet, because of this, he thinks:
"The benefit born of my meditative attainment, together with its basis, is declining."
And because of that, he turns the mind away [from it].
In this way, when concentration is declining, the meditator must fully understand the error.
(4.2.4.1.3) How is non-error to be fully understood when concentration is declining?
In this case, a certain person becomes satisfied with the attainment of the first dhyāna and does not strive for what is higher; he relishes that state.
For him, there arises a perception and mental attention accompanied by desire, through which he falls away from the attainment proximate to the realm of desire.
This is his misfortune.
And he regards that [attainment] as being subject to misfortune.
In this regard, he must fully understand the absence of error.
Furthermore, by means of that meditative absorption, he exalts himself and disparages others:
"I am one who has attained the meditative absorptions (dhyāna-samāpatti), whereas others are not so.
Such a perception and mental attention (saṃjñā-manasikāra) accompanied by desire arises in him;
and because he increases and solidifies that obsession (paryavasthāna), he falls away from that concentration (samādhi).
And that is his misfortune;
he perceives it as misfortune.
Furthermore, he becomes a possessor of the attainment of meditative absorption (dhyāna-samāpatti).
Because of that, other kings or royal ministers esteem him, and they honor him.
Having emerged from that concentration, he reflects upon what is associated with it;
thus, there arises in him a perception and mental attention accompanied by sensual desire.
And because one increases that obsession as previously described,
a meditator must thus understand non-perversion regarding the decline of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, the second non-perversion is to be understood as the opposite of the first perversion.
H 80b6; C 342c9 (4.2.4.2) These constitute the four turnings based on error and non-error.
H 80b7; C 342c12 (4.2.5.0) A meditator who practices the fourfold investigation investigates concentration through four aspects:
“This concentration belongs to the stage of decline,” up to “it belongs to the stage leading to penetration.”
How, then, does one investigate?
"This is inferior, this is superior, this is more superior, this is most superior," respectively.
How, moreover, is this done?
H 80b7; C 342c16 (4.2.5.1) Here, this meditator has emerged from the first dhyāna but is not yet desirous of re-entering that dhyāna.

He does not attend to those aspects, signs, and marks; rather, the perceptions and mental attentions associated with sensual desire arise as previously described, and even for one who has emerged, there is recollection and relishing.
At that time, the meditator should examine the deficiency of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, when the meditator has emerged from the first dhyāna, he receives a teaching of the Dharma conducive to the first dhyāna.
He then correctly and thoroughly grasps the signs (*nimitta*) of those factors, such as the aspects (*ākāra*) of the first dhyāna, so that there is stability for the dhyāna he has attained.
This is the mindfulness that accords with that [state], belonging to the stage of stability.
At that time, it should be understood:
"This concentration of mine is excellent; my concentration remains stable; it does not decline, nor does it progress toward distinction or penetration."
Furthermore, another meditator, having emerged from [the first dhyāna], receives a teaching of the Dharma that is concordant with the second dhyāna.
Having heard it, perceptions and mental attentions associated with the path to the attainment of the second dhyāna arise in him. At that time, he investigates:
"This concentration of mine is superior; it does not lead to decline, nor does it remain static, but rather leads to distinction, though not yet to penetration.
Having emerged from that state, he hears a teaching of the Dharma associated with the truths of suffering and so forth.
Upon hearing it, perceptions and mental attentions associated with the truths of suffering and so forth, which are conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), arise in him.
At that time, he investigates: "This concentration of mine is most excellent; it does not lead to decline, nor to stagnation, nor to distinction, but rather proceeds toward penetration.
As it was said: [H 81a4; C 343a7 (4.2.6)]
There is the eye and visible forms, up to the mind and mental phenomena; yet, furthermore, a monk does not experience these phenomena as they truly exist and are present.
He does not experience them even while possessing perception, let alone while being without perception.
How, then, is this so?
In this case, a monk dwells having attained the first dhyāna.
By means of that, his eyes— and so on, up to— mental phenomena become overcome through revulsion and mastery.

He does not have the perception of "eye" regarding the eye, yet he is one who possesses perception; and so on, up to: he does not have the perception of "phenomena" regarding phenomena, yet he is one who possesses perception.
How does he possess perception?
He attends to the eye and the other [faculties] as suffering, or as an origin, or as a disease, and so forth.
He does not experience those dharmas by way of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
and so on up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
And this is the untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manaskāra*).
How is it that one who is without perception does not experience?
Because of non-attention toward all signs, one attends to cessation as peace.
That perception which is free from all signs is what is intended here by "non-perception," as well as the total non-occurrence of all perceptions for one who has entered the attainment of cessation.
(4.2.7.0) There are four expositions of the path.
(4.2.7.1.1) How does one, seated in that manner, investigate and thoroughly examine phenomena?
Here, a monk is an attainer of the first dhyāna and so forth, yet he has not yet seen the truths.
And by means of that hearing of the true Dharma and extensive learning, it is accomplished.
As soon as he sits down, relying upon that samādhi, he brings about the clear realization of the truths, beginning with suffering. Relying upon higher mind, he applies himself to higher wisdom.
Furthermore, he understands suffering as it really is, up to the path; yet he is not yet an attainer of the first dhyāna and so forth.
Even while sitting down, he investigates phenomena.
Relying on that very [attainment] as the basis for higher wisdom, he applies himself to the yoga of higher mind.
(H 81b1; C 343a27) He is one who has attained both in the third [stage]. For him, both calm abiding and insight become blended and proceed in equal union.
(4.2.7.1.4) Fourth: He has already previously obtained the first dhyāna and so forth;
however, it was not by means of this hearing of the true Dharma or by great learning that he achieved it.
He hears the Dharma from the Teacher or from some other guru, either concerning the Truths or regarding the abandonment of the remaining fetters.
Either by fully realizing the truths or by attaining arhatship,
he experiences a sublime, wholesome joy associated with renunciation.
With his mind restrained by that upliftment through the Dharma, he sits down.
Seated thus, he stabilizes that mind by means of dwelling in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and attainment (*samāpatti*).

In this regard, the first instruction on the path concerns the accomplishment of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); the second and third concern the accomplishment of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); and the fourth concerns the accomplishment of both.
H 81b3; C 343b7 (4.2.8.0) There are four primary purifications, so called because they are the principal factors for purification. What is purification? What is the primary factor?
The fulfillment of those ethical disciplines (*śīla*) and so forth that have been acquired, attained, and brought forth, as well as the benefit [they provide], is this purity.
That exertion of vigor (*vīryārambha*) by which one fulfills what is not yet fulfilled is the primary [factor].
What is the fulfillment of ethical discipline?
What is assistance?

Here, a certain person dwells possessed of ethical discipline, restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa, yet he is not perfected in conduct and range, nor does he perceive danger in even the slightest faults. His ethical discipline is thus incomplete.
When, however, all this comes to pass, then it becomes complete;
this is the fulfillment of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
