Through long-term practice of this, for one who dwells with the doors of the senses guarded, there arises—in detail, up to—the state of being absorbed in that ethical discipline and abiding in its very nature; this is the benefit (*anugraha*).
H 81b5; C 343b17 (4.2.8.2) The fulfillment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*):
if one attains the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*) in either the fourth *dhyāna* or [a lower stage], that is fulfillment. Prior to that, it is incomplete.

What is favor (anugraha)? It is the subsequent purification of the meditative concentration (samādhi) that has been attained; and his concentration does not become suppressed by formative forces (saṃskāra), and so forth in detail.
H 81b5; C 343b22 (4.2.8.3) What is the fulfillment of view? What is the benefit? Right view arises from the influence of another’s voice and from appropriate mental attention.
By means of that [insight], one understands suffering up to the path, yet not as it truly is;
as long as this is so, right view is not fulfilled.
But when one understands it as it truly is, then it becomes fulfilled.
Furthermore, favor (*anugraha*) is described as:
"at another time, through the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*)," and so forth. What is the fulfillment of liberation (*vimukti-paripūri*)?
What is the favor?

That liberation from passion and the other defilements through the knowledge and vision of one in training is incomplete; that which is through the knowledge and vision of one beyond training is complete.
Furthermore, the favor [of the teaching] is this:
as he practices and as he dwells, there is no falling away from that dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
The Sūtra states: "A monk who has set out for the purification of the mind should, from time to time, attend to five signs."

One who is engaged in higher consciousness (*adhicitta*) and has entered upon the path to the purification of the mind encounters obstacles in the form of unwholesome thoughts concerning sensual desires and thoughts concerning kin and so forth.
Furthermore, that person is of three types, distinguished by whether their conduct regarding these thoughts is weak, middling, or intense.
(4.2.9.1.1) For the first [type of person], there is a non-arising of those discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) because of mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward another cause.
(4.2.9.1.2) For the second, it is due to seeing the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) of discursive thought, or due to non-recollection and non-mental-attention (*asmṛtyamanasikāra*).
How does one practice non-recollection and non-mental-attention?
(4.2.9.1.3) Through such means as the stabilization of the internal mind,
for the third type of person, there is not at all from the very beginning a complete non-occurrence [of discursive thought].

Therefore, he must gradually effect the loosening of the formative forces of discursive thought (*vitarka-saṃskāra*), so that by the pacification of the coarse [thought], there may be gradual suppression (*viṣkambhaṇa*).
Even so, being unable [to proceed], he causes the mind to feel revulsion and terror toward the paths of discursive thought (*vitarka*) and the objects of discursive thought.

Having caused revulsion, with a mind accompanied by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), through frequent mental attention, he torments and restrains that mind associated with discursive thought.
These constitute the five modes for these three types of persons.

Regarding what was said by the Blessed One in the *Pāṃsudhāvaka-sūtra* concerning the purification of the mind through its analogy with the purification of gold (*jātarūpa*): how is that to be understood? For the purification of gold is threefold:
purification from secondary defilements (*upakleśa*), purification through gathering (*saṃgraha*), and purification of workability (*karmaṇyatā*).

In that regard, purification from secondary afflictions (*upakleśa-viśuddhi*) refers to the removal of gross, medium, and subtle secondary afflictions from gold situated within its lineage (*gotrastha*), until only pure golden sand remains. In that regard, purification through gathering (*saṃgraha-viśuddhi*) refers to the revolving and turning back of those very sands.
In that regard, the purification of workability (*karmaṇyatā*) results from the cleansing of defects such as fragility in what has been refined. (H 82a4;

C 343c24) Therein, just as gold exists in its natural state (*gotrastha*), so too should one who has entered the practice for the purification of mind (*cetoviśuddhipratipannaka*)—who is capable of attaining *parinirvāṇa* through revulsion (*abhinirveda*)—be regarded as existing in the lineage (*gotrastha*).
Furthermore, from what point is he considered one who has entered the practice for the purification of mind?
From the point at which one acquires faith, by means of which one goes forth.
In both the state of a householder and the state of going forth, there are three secondary afflictions:
the coarse ones and so forth.
In this regard, there are two things that create an obstacle to renunciation for a householder:
unwholesome occupations, which consist of misconduct of body and speech that serves as a basis for pleasure, and evil views, such as:
"There are no Arhats in the world who have attained the right path."
This [distraction] acts as an obstacle to the attainment of faith prior to its acquisition. (H 82a5;
C 344a2, 4.2.10.2.2.2) Discursive thoughts of sensual desire and the like are obstacles to the delight of one who has gone forth. (H 82a6;
C 344a2, 4.2.10.2.2.3) Discursive thoughts of kin and the like are obstacles to the continuity of the cultivation of wholesome qualities for one who finds delight [in them].

Through their abandonment and by accomplishing the continuity of the cultivation of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*), the mind becomes pure, accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*), just as pure gold sand remains unrefined.
This is the purification of the mind from secondary afflictions (*upakleśa-viśuddhi*) by way of its similarity to refined gold (*jātarūpa-sārūpyeṇa*).
When he, through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, this is the purification of the mind through integration (*saṃgraha-viśuddhi*).
Because it is comprised within the concentration free from applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra-samādhi*), it is like gold that has been refined through repeated heating and hammering.

As it is said in detail: "If the concentration is not suppressed by formative forces (*saṃskāra*)," this is the purification of the mind’s adaptability (*karmaṇyatā*) regarding the phenomena to be directly known, because it can transform them according to one's wish, just as gold is freed from defects such as brittleness.
H 82b1; C 344a13 (4.2.11) It has been stated that one should again attend to three signs.
From time to time, one should attend to calm (*śamatha*) and the others, but not exclusively, for the sake of counteracting laxity (*laya*) and so forth.

In that regard, for one who has not yet performed the preparatory cultivation (*parikarman*), the cultivation of only one side of either calm or exertion (*pragraha*) is a sign of laxity or excitement.
This is the path of application (*prayogamārga*).
From time to time, there is the sign of equanimity (*upekṣānimitta*); this is the time of the path of completion (*niṣpattimārga*).

Because one cultivates only that single part and does not perform the analytical investigation of dependent origination and the [four] truths, the mind is not correctly concentrated for the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*).
Furthermore, he does not realize the truths that have not yet been realized, or, even when they have been realized, he does not attain the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

The path for the perfection of concentration is [taught] by two [factors], while the path for the destruction of the outflows based on concentration is briefly elucidated by the third, through the mental attention (*manasikāra*) to all [objects] from time to time.
(H 82b3; C 344a25) There are four factors that lead to the preservation of the teaching:
Seclusion, cultivation, the fruit of cultivation, and the non-confusion of the teaching.
(4.2.12.1) Among these, seclusion consists of forest retreats, the roots of trees, and empty dwellings.
(4.2.12.2) Cultivation:
Having gone there, two qualities should be cultivated:
serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
It is said that when serenity is practiced and supported by insight, one is liberated; this is as when one becomes an attainer of the first dhyāna up to the fourth.
Relying upon that concentration, he understands suffering as it truly is, up to the path.
Having attained that insight (*vipaśyanā*), his mind is liberated from the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing.
How is it that insight, when cultivated, brings liberation by relying upon tranquility (*śamatha*)?
In this case, a certain person understands suffering as it truly is, up to and including the Path.
Relying upon that higher wisdom, he generates meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
Having attained that tranquility (*śamatha*), his mind is liberated from the afflictions (*kleśa*) that are to be abandoned through cultivation.
H 82b5; C 344b8 (4.2.12.3) Thus, when one is permeated by calm abiding and insight, one is liberated within the elements (*dhātu*).
Therein, the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are to be abandoned by seeing is the element of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*).
The abandonment of those to be abandoned by cultivation is the element of dispassion (*virāgadhātu*).
The cessation of all substrates is the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).
This is the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanāphala*).
In this regard, there is no confusion regarding the teaching (*śāsana*):
The meaning of the Teacher and the meaning of his disciples flow together and coincide, word with word and syllable with syllable;
it is not as among the followers of other sects, where various and manifold divergent views are perceived.
That is to say, by the "initial words" means by the preceding words.

If the second person were to be questioned by the very same means as the first, then if the first were questioned starting from the aggregates (*skandha*), the second might be questioned starting from something else; thus, they would not be consistent with the initial terms.
H 82b6; (C 344b20) (Ω) The *Samāhitā Bhūmi* in the *Yogācārabhūmi* is completed.
